But see what fruits he first receives in the land of promise: then, it says, "they ate" first "of the fruits" from the region of palms, and "they ate" first "the unleavened bread." You see, therefore, that when we have first departed from the journey of this world, if we rightly follow Jesus, the first thing that meets us is the palm of victory, and, when the "leaven of malice and wickedness" has been cast away, the "unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" is prepared for us.
On the Gospel of Luke 6.22

"And Jesus said to them: 'I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.' " He desired first of all to eat the typical Passover with his disciples and thus to reveal the mystery of his passion to the world, so that the judge of the ancient and lawful Passover would emerge and forbid this to be displayed to have pertained to the type of its dispensation by further carnal teaching but would demonstrate instead through the passing shadow that the light of the true Passover has now come. The time and order of Joshua finishing the manna beautifully prefigures this, where it is written: "And they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening in the plains of Jericho, and they ate from the fruit of the earth on the next day, unleavened bread from the grain of the land of the same year. And the manna ceased after they ate of the fruit of the earth, nor did the children of Israel use that food any more." For, when Moses died, Joshua restored the people whom he had provided with manna for a time across the Jordan, by which food he himself was also restored, even though he knew and formerly tasted of the fruit of the promised land. Thereafter, he crossed the Jordan, circumcised with knives made of stone and did not take the customary manna for three and one half months, until the day of Passover. In fact, Joshua was ordained leader when Moses died because Christ was incarnated when the law had been corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees. Joshua fed with and was fed by manna across the Jordan because, until the time of his baptism, the Lord observed the ceremonies of the law and wanted them to be observed by everyone else. After they had crossed the Jordan, Joshua circumcised the people with knives made from stone because the Savior celebrated the grace of baptism with thoughts that the law, in its severity, had been unable to cut off the attractions of faith. And for three and one half years [after his baptism], although provoking gradual movement toward the promised heaven, Christ does not cease to observe the sacraments of the law, as though to be nourished with the customary manna, until, while eating the desired Passover with his disciples at a foreordained time, as morning was breaking, he finally offers the most pure sacrament of his body and blood, consecrated on the altar of the cross for imbuing the faithful, as though it were the unleavened bread of the promised land.
HOMILIES ON NUMBERS 27.11

And therefore one must beware and act carefully, so that you may knowingly discern the kind of visions, just as Joshua the son of Nun also, when he saw a vision, knowing that there was temptation in this, at once inquires of him who appeared and says: "Are you ours or of our adversaries?" So then the advancing soul also, when it has come to this point, that it now begins to have discernment of visions, will thereby be proved to be spiritual, if it knows how to discern all things. Finally, therefore, among the spiritual gifts as well, one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is said to be the discernment of spirits.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 6.2

"And it came to pass," it says, "when Jesus was at Jericho, that looking up with his eyes he saw a man standing over against him, and a drawn sword was in his hand. And Jesus, drawing near, said to him: are you ours, or of our adversaries? And he said: I am the prince of the host of the Lord's power; now I have come." "Looking up," then, "with his eyes he sees the prince of the Lord's host," as one who had not "looked up" before, but only then, when he was about to see the "prince of the Lord's host." Yet when Jesus had seen him, he did not see him as a common man, but understood that he was a certain power. Nevertheless he is not yet certain whether the one who appears is one from the divine powers or from the contrary ones, and therefore he asks and inquires, saying: "are you ours, or of our adversaries?"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 6.2

And he says: "I am the prince of the host of the Lord's power; now I have come." And when he had heard this, Jesus worshiped and said: "Lord, what do you command your servant?" What is it that Jesus teaches us through this? That, without doubt, which the Apostle says: "do not believe every spirit, but test whether it is of God." Jesus, then, recognized not only that "he is of God," but that he is God; for he would not have worshiped had he not recognized God. For who else is the "prince of the host of the Lord's powers" but our Lord Jesus Christ? For all the host of heaven, whether angels or archangels, or powers "or dominions or principalities or authorities," all these, which were made through him, do military service under him as prince, who is the prince of princes and who bestows principalities upon princes. For it is he who says in the Gospel: "be one having authority over ten cities," and to another: "be one having authority over five cities." It is he who, "having received the kingdom, returned."
The Proof of the Gospel (Book V), Chapter 19

The same words, you will remember, were said by the same Lord to Moses at the beginning of the vision of the Bush, for Scripture says: "And when the Lord saw that he drew nigh to see, He called him from the midst of the Bush, saying, Moses, Moses, come not near here; loose thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."

So, then, the command that was given shews that the God Who answered on both occasions was one and the same. Though here He prophesies through the Chief and Captain of His power, and to Moses by the vision of the angel. And of the heavenly armies, celestial powers and invisible spirits, holy angels and archangels ministering to God the King of kings and the Lord of lords (as Daniel says: "Thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him"), what other could be highest of all but the Word of God, His Firstborn Wisdom, His Divine Offspring? Rightly, then, He is here called Chief Captain of the Power of the Lord, as also elsewhere "Angel of Great Counsel," "Throned with the Father," "Eternal and Great High Priest." And it has been proved that the same Being is both Lord and God, and Christ anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness. Thus, appearing to Abraham by the oak in human form, He reveals Himself in a calm and peaceful guise, foreshowing by it His future Coming to save mankind; He appeared to Jacob, as to an athlete and a champion destined to wrestle with enemies, in the form of a man, and to Moses and the people in the form of cloud and fire, and led them, shewing Himself terrible and shadowy.

And as Joshua, the successor of Moses, was about to fight against the former possessors of Palestine his enemies, foreign and most ungodly races, He rightly appears to him with a sword drawn and pointed against the enemy, shewing by the vision that He Himself is about to attack the ungodly with an unseen sword and with divine power, the fellow-soldier and the fellow-combatant of His people. Wherefore He gives Himself the name of Chief and Captain of the Lord to suit the occasion.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 6.3

But meanwhile let us see what the present reading suggests. Jesus is at Jericho; the enemies still hold the city and are not yet conquered. Yet already it is said to Jesus: "loose the shoe from your feet; for the place in which you stand is holy ground." And how is Jericho "holy ground," which is held by the enemies? But perhaps this is what is indicated: that wherever the "prince of the host of the Lord's power" comes, he sanctifies the place, because Jericho itself was not a holy place; but because the "prince of the Lord's host" came there, the place is called "holy." I even dare something further, and say that even where Moses stood, of itself it was not a holy place, but because the Lord stood with Moses, the presence of the Lord had sanctified the place, and therefore it is said to him: "loose the strap of your shoe: for the place in which you stand is holy ground." Whence we too, if by our life and merits we draw near to the Lord and are made worthy for God to stand by us, it is said also to us that we should loose from the feet of our soul whatever bond of mortality is bound to them. For these are the "feet" which Jesus "washes"; which, "unless he washes them, we shall have no part with him." So then, if we loose from our soul and senses every bond of mortal care, immediately God too will gladly be present and stand by us.

n: The Lord, in the person of the angel, who appeared to Josue, as he was praying in silent meditation, or reconnoitring the city of Jericho, chap. v. 13. (Haydock) --- Men. People of the different nations had come to defend the city, chap. xxiv. 11.
Men. These went first. Afterwards the priests bore the ark, which was followed by all the people. (Calmet) --- The procession began on a Sunday. (Rabbins)

Jubilee. (Numbers x. 2.) The number seven, is often used to express an indefinite number. But here a particular stress is laid upon it. See Masius. As, on the 7th year the Hebrews regained the possessions which they had sold: so now they assert their rights to the land of Chanaan. The sound of the trumpets announced joyful tidings to them. (Menochius)

Tune, with certain modulations, continued for a long time, Numbers x. 5. (Haydock) --- Ground. The Rabbins say they sink in, so that the ruins might not impede the march of the army. Some think only a large breach was made, opposite to the Israelites, as the house of Rahab upon the walls was preserved. (Calmet)

He said. Some manuscripts and Hebrew editions have, "they said," though the points shew it must be singular, whatever Michaelis may object in favour of the Masora. Leudsen foolishly admits here a double literal sense. (Kennicott) (Haydock)
There. This singular procession served to exercise the obedience of the people, and to teach them to despise the enemy, who durst not come out to attack them, though many were unarmed. (Calmet)

Seventh day. The Jews say it was the sabbath; but of this there is no proof. Marcion hence took occasion to accuse God of inconsistency, as he forbad all working, and yet ordered the people to go round Jericho on a sabbath day. But Tertullian (iv. 12,) answers very well, that servile work is forbidden, and not the works of God or of religion, and God may change the ceremonial law as he thinks proper. (Calmet) --- Sabbato opera humana prohibentur non divina. (Du Hamel)

Said, or "had said," when he gave the people the sound of the trumpet for a sign (Haydock) when they were to shout, ver. 5. He probably gave the regulations respecting the plunder of the city, before the army left the camp. (Calmet)

An anathema. That is, a thing accursed and devoted to utter destruction. (Challoner) --- Only the metal that was found, was consecrated to the Lord, (ver. 19,) and the family of Rahab saved. In devoting things, the person who laid on the curse, might extend its operation as he pleased. On some occasions, all was to be destroyed; on others, some things were preserved, Deuteronomy ii. 34., and Leviticus xxvii. 21. (Calmet) --- This first city, which the Israelites attacked, was treated with peculiar severity, to terrify the rest.
Forbidden, transgression, sin. Hebrew has always anathema. (Haydock)

Treasures, probably in the tabernacle. See Numbers xxxi. 48. God claims the first-fruits of the booty, as an acknowledgment that he granted the victory, (Calmet) and all the riches of the country, to his people. (Haydock)

Men. Hebrew, "boys;" a name given to people advanced in years. --- Camp. A respect for the majesty of God, would not permit the Israelites to introduce unbelievers into the camp. They were first instructed, and then the men were circumcised, and the women received baptism. (Calmet)

Day. Rahab prefigured the wild olive tree, which St. Paul says was engrafted on the good olive tree, (Romans xi. 24,) and which will remain till the end of the world. (Theodoret, q. 8.) She married Salmon, of the tribe of Juda, and became the ancestor of David and of the Messias. (Calmet)

Cursed, &c. Jericho, in the mystical sense, signifies iniquity; the sounding of the trumpets by the priests, signifies the preaching of the word of God; by which the walls of Jericho are thrown down, when sinners are converted: and a dreadful curse will light on them who build them up again. (Challoner) --- Gates. Some copies of the Septuagint insert here that the curse fell upon Azan (Hiel) of Bethel, 3 Kings xvi. 34. Before his time, there was a city of palm-trees, or Jericho, built in the neighbourhood. (Josephus, Jewish Wars v. 4.) Though Hiel was so severely punished, no one made any scruple to live there. Elias and Jesus Christ himself honoured the place with their presence. The city is now almost in ruins, and the territory uncultivated. Ancient history mentions similar imprecations against obnoxious cities. Thus the Romans cursed the rebuilders of Carthage, and Agamemnon followed "the ancient custom," says Strabo, (xiii.) laying a curse upon those who should rebuild the city of Troy. The Ionians and Greeks forbad those temples to be re-established, which the Persians had destroyed, that they might remain eternal monuments of the impiety of the latter, and of the hatred which subsisted between the two nations. (Pausanias in Phoc.) (Calmet)

f: AN ANSWER TO THE JEWS 4

But the Jews are sure to say that ever since this precept was given through Moses, the observance has been binding. But it is clear according to the text that the precept was not eternal or spiritual but temporary, which would one day cease. In short, so true is it that it is not in the exemption from work of the sabbath—that is, of the seventh day—that the celebration of this solemnity is to consist, that Joshua the son of Nun, at the time that he was reducing the city Jericho by war, stated that he had received from God a precept to order the people that priests should carry the ark of the testament of God seven days, making the circuit of the city; and thus, when the seventh day's circuit had been performed, the walls of the city would spontaneously fall. This was done. When the space of the seventh day was finished, just as was predicted, down fell the walls of the city. [By this] it is manifestly shown that in the number of the seven days there intervened a Sabbath day. For seven days, whenever they may have commenced, must necessarily include within them a Sabbath day; on which day not only must the priests have worked, but the city must have been made a prey by the edge of the sword by all the people of Israel.
On the Creation of the World

Jesus also, the son of Nave, the successor of Moses, himself broke the Sabbath-day; for on the Sabbath-day he commanded the children of Israel to go round the walls of the city of Jericho with trumpets, and declare war against the aliens.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.4

But let us see what it is that is indicated in what follows. For Jesus says: "keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest perhaps you covet and take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of the children of Israel accursed, and crush yourselves and the whole synagogue of the Lord." Such is what is indicated in these words: see that you have nothing worldly in you, that you do not carry along with you into the church worldly ways, nor vices, nor the shiftiness of the world; but let all worldly conduct be "accursed" to you. Do not mix worldly things with divine, do not insert the business of the age into the secret things of the church. This is what John too sounds forth with the trumpet of his epistle, saying: "do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world." And Paul likewise: "do not," he says, "be conformed to this world." For those who do these things "take of the accursed thing." But also those who, for example, though they are Christians, celebrate the festivals of the nations, bring "the accursed thing" into the churches. Those who search out the lives and deeds of men from the courses of the stars, who inquire into the flights of birds and other things of this kind, which were formerly observed in the world, bring "the accursed thing" from Jericho into the church, and defile the camp of the Lord, and cause the people of God to be conquered. But there are also many other sins through which "the accursed thing" from Jericho is brought into the church; through which the people of God is conquered and laid low by its enemies. Or does not the Apostle also enjoin these very things when he says: "a little leaven corrupts the whole lump"?
LETTER 47

And when temples, idols, groves, and other things of the sort are authorized to be torn down, although it is evident when we do this that we are not honoring but despising them, still we should not take away anything for private, or at least personal, use so that our purpose in tearing down must be manifest as devotion, not cupidity. However, when such things are turned over for public, not private or personal use, as when they are used to honor the true God, that same holds true for things as for people, when they turn from sacrilege and impiety to the true religion. God is understood to have taught this by those texts which you quoted, as when he ordered wood from the grove of foreign gods to be brought for a holocaust and ordered that all the gold, silver and brass vessels be carried into the treasury of the Lord.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.1

Jericho is overthrown by the trumpets of the priests. For at once, as soon as the blast of the trumpets sounded loudly, the whole circuit of walls was thrown down. We had already said before too that Jericho holds the figure of the present age, whose strength and defenses we see destroyed by the priestly trumpets. For the firmness and defenses which this world used as walls were the worship of idols, the deceit of divinations administered by the craft of demons, the fabrications of augurs and soothsayers and magicians — by all of which this world was fenced about as by the strongest walls. Moreover it was also fortified by the diverse doctrines of the philosophers and by the most lofty assertions of their disputations, as by certain tall and sturdy towers. But when our Lord Jesus Christ came, whose coming that former son of Nave prefigured, he sends his priests, the Apostles, bearing "trumpets of beaten metal," the magnificent and heavenly teaching of preaching. With the priestly trumpet Matthew first sounded loudly in his Gospel; Mark also, Luke, and John each sang with their priestly trumpets; Peter too resounds with the two trumpets of his epistles; James also and Jude. Nonetheless John also adds still further to sound the trumpet through his epistles, and Luke by describing the deeds of the Apostles. But last of all comes that one who said: "for I think that God has set forth us Apostles as the last," and, thundering in the trumpets of his fourteen epistles, he cast down to the very foundations the walls of Jericho and all the engines of idolatry and the doctrines of the philosophers.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.2

I am indeed also moved by this, which the narrative relates: that not only did the priests sound the trumpets so that the walls of Jericho might fall, but also that, "when the voice of the trumpet was heard," it is said that "the whole people howled with a great howling," or, as it stands in other copies, "shouted for joy with a great jubilation." And although this word may seem to have been improperly translated — for in the Greek it is written ἀλαλαγμός, which properly signifies neither jubilation nor howling, but rather denotes that shout by which, in time of war, an army raising a united cry is accustomed with one mind to exhort itself to battle — yet in the Scriptures this word is customarily written down as jubilation rather than as howling, as there: "shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth," and again: "blessed is the people that knows the jubilation." And this saying too moves me: what so great a work this is, that it "makes the people blessed." He did not say "blessed is the people" that works righteousness, or "blessed is the people" that knows the mysteries, or that knows the reckoning of heaven and earth and the stars, but he says, "blessed is the people that knows the jubilation." In other places the fear of God makes one blessed, but it makes only a single man blessed; for so it says: "blessed is the man that fears the Lord." Elsewhere too more are made blessed, such as the "poor in spirit," or the "meek," or the "peacemakers," or the "pure in heart." But this beatitude is lavished abroad, and by some cause of blessedness, I know not what, so great a thing is here indicated, that it makes the "whole people" alike "blessed" — the people, however, "that has known the jubilation." Hence it seems to me that this jubilation indicates a certain disposition of concord and unanimity. And if it should fall upon two or three of Christ's disciples, whatever they ask in the name of the Savior, the heavenly Father grants to them. But if the beatitude be so great that the whole people remains harmonious and of one mind, so that "all say the same thing, continuing in the same understanding and in the same judgment," then, when such a people lifts up its voice with one accord, there will come to pass that which is written in the Acts of the Apostles, that "there was a great earthquake," where at that time "the Apostles were praying with one accord together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus"; and when the earthquake has occurred, all things that are earthly will be destroyed and will fall, and the world itself will be overturned. Hear, finally, our Lord and Savior exhorting his soldiers to this very thing, how he says: "be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." Under that leader, then, the world has already been overcome by us, and its walls have collapsed — the walls on which the men of the age relied. But each one of us too ought to accomplish these things within his very self. You have within you Jesus as your leader through faith; make for yourself "trumpets of beaten metal," if you are a priest; nay rather, since you are a priest — for you have been made a "royal race," and a "holy priesthood" has been spoken of concerning you — make for yourself "trumpets of beaten metal" out of the holy Scriptures; from there draw your meanings, from there your words; for it is on this account that they are called trumpets of beaten metal. Sound upon them, that is, "sing in psalms, in hymns, in spiritual songs," sound in the prophetic sacraments, in the mysteries of the law, in the apostolic doctrines. And if you sound upon such trumpets and carry the ark of the testament around "seven times," that is, if you do not separate the mystical precepts of the law from the evangelical trumpets, if you also exact from your very self the harmony of jubilation — that is, if the people of your thoughts and senses, which is within you, always utters a concordant and consonant voice, and you do not sometimes speak the truth and sometimes stain yourself with a lie by flattering a powerful person; if remissness does not at times make you fawning, and anger at times make you savage; if you are not found arrogant toward the lowly and humble before the proud; in short, if a battle is no longer waged within you while "the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh" — if these things now sound in unison and are in concord within you, send forth the voice of jubilation, since for you the world has been destroyed and cast down. Such, I suppose, was also that man who confidently said: "but far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.3

Yet something in the passage still moves me: I seem to have perceived too little concerning the jubilation, to have said lowly things about great matters. At the coming of Jesus the walls of Jericho were overturned; at the coming of my Lord Jesus the world is conquered. Yet how the world is conquered, I would like to know more plainly and to understand more clearly the things that are said. I myself, who teach you, wish to learn together with you. Let us commonly take Paul to ourselves as our teacher; for he is the fellow-initiate of Christ, who can show us how Christ conquered the world. Hear him, then, saying: "that which was contrary to us, he took it out of the midst, nailing it to his cross; and stripping off the principalities and powers, he led them openly, triumphing over them on the wood of the cross." From these words, then, I understand this: that the heavenly powers, seeing the battle of Jesus, seeing the contrary "principalities and powers" stripped of their powers, seeing "the strong man bound and his vessels plundered," sounded their heavenly trumpets, because, when "the prince of this world" was bound, the world was conquered, and the heavenly army gave forth the voice of jubilation in the triumph of Christ. Truly, then, blessed is the people of the nations, which has come to know such a jubilation as this of the heavenly army, and which recognizes the mysteries and believes.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 6.4

But let us see what things follow. Jericho is surrounded; it must be taken by storm. How, then, is Jericho stormed? No sword is drawn against it, no battering-ram is directed, nor are missiles hurled; only the priestly trumpets are employed, and by these the walls of Jericho are undermined. We frequently find in the Scriptures that Jericho is set down as a figure of this world. For in the Gospel too, that which is said, that "a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers," was without doubt an image of that Adam who was thrust from paradise into the exile of this world. And the "blind men" too, who were in Jericho, to whom Jesus came to make them see, bore the figure of those who in this world were pressed down by the blindness of ignorance, to whom the Son of God came. This Jericho, then — that is, this world — is to fall; for the consummation of the age has long since been made widely known in the sacred volumes. How, then, will its consummation be given? By what instruments? "By the voices," it says, "of the trumpets." Of which "trumpets"? Let Paul disclose to you the secret of this mystery; listen to what he himself says: "the trumpet shall sound," he says, "and the dead who are in Christ shall rise incorruptible," and: "the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven." Then, therefore, Jesus our Lord, with the trumpets, conquers Jericho and lays it low, so that from it the harlot alone is saved, and all her house.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 5.10.126

And did Joshua, the son of Nun, err in recognizing the leader of the heavenly host? But after he believed, he forthwith conquered, being found worthy to triumph in the battle of faith. Again, he did not lead forth his armed ranks into the fight, nor did he overthrow the ramparts of the enemy's walls, with battering rams or other engines of war, but with the sound of the seven trumpets of the priests. Thus the blare of the trumpet and the badge of the priest brought a cruel war to an end.
City of God 10.17

Besides the signs just mentioned and the voices which could be heard in the neighborhood of the ark, other miraculous testimonies to the law were witnessed. For example, when the people were entering the promised land and the ark was crossing the Jordan, the river stood still above them and flowed on below them so that the ark and the people had a dry place for crossing. Again, when they came upon the first hostile city where the religion was pagan and polytheistic, the ark was carried around it seven times and then, suddenly, the walls collapsed before a hand was raised or a battering ram was used.
LETTER 55

So the walls of that city, called Jericho, which in the Hebrew tongue is said to mean moon, fell when they had been encircled seven times by the ark of the covenant. What, then, does the announcement of the kingdom of heaven portend—signified by the encircling of the ark—except that all the battlements of mortal life, that is, all the hope of this world, which is opposed to the hope of the world to come, will be destroyed by the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit, working through the free will? For, those walls fell of their own accord, not by any violent push of the ark in its circuit. There are other references in Scripture which suggest the church to us under the symbolism of the moon, as it makes its pilgrimage in this mortal life, amid toils and labors, far from that Jerusalem whose citizens are the holy angels.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.5

But let us now see the things that follow. Jericho having been overturned, Rahab the harlot alone is saved. For thus it is written of her: "and Rahab the harlot and all the house of her father, Jesus made alive; and she was joined to Israel unto this present day." I would like to inquire of the Jews, and of those who are indeed called Christians but still keep a Jewish sense in the Scriptures, how they explain that "Rahab the harlot was joined to the house of Israel unto this present day." How is Rahab said to be "joined unto this present day"? For it is the custom of holy Scripture to say this of those things which remain unto the end either of life or of the age. For example, as it says: "this is the father of the Moabites unto this present day," which signifies unto the end of the age. And again in the Gospel it is said that "this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this present day," that is, as long as the age stands. But how is Rahab, a woman, said to be "joined to the house of Israel unto this present day"? Is a succession of posterity ascribed to a mother, so that she may seem to be preserved in the renewal of offspring? Or is it rather to be understood that she "has been joined" and made a companion to the true Israel "unto this present day"? And if you wish to see more plainly how "Rahab is joined to Israel," look at how "the branch of the wild olive is grafted into the root of the good olive tree," and you will understand how those who have been grafted into the faith of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are rightly said to be "set beside" and "joined to Israel unto this present day," because in their "root" we, "the branches of the wild olive" taken from among the nations — we who once played the harlot, worshiping "wood and stone" in place of the true God — "have been set beside them unto this present day," and, on account of faith in Christ, we have been made "above," while that people which has remained unbelieving has been made "below," according to the prophecy of Deuteronomy. If anyone, then, has within himself Christ, who is "the head of all," this one is made "into the head"; for they denied Christ Jesus and were made into the tail, and those who were "first" have been made "last."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 6.4

"The Lord" our Jesus "shall come," then, "and shall come at the voice of the trumpets." But even now let us pray that he may come and destroy this "world," which "is set in wickedness," and "all the things that are in the world," because "everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes." May he destroy those things, may he now, this very moment, dissolve them, but may he save this one alone, who received his spies, who received his Apostles in faith and obedience and set them in the upper rooms, and may he join and unite this harlot with the house of Israel. But let us now not bring up again nor reckon against her the old fault. Once she was a harlot, but now she is joined as "a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ." Hear the Apostle saying of her: "for I have determined this very thing, to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ." From her too was that very one who said: "for we also were once foolish, unbelieving, going astray, serving desires and various pleasures." Do you wish to learn yet more fully how the harlot is now no longer a harlot? Hear Paul saying further: "and such indeed you were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God." For that she might be able to escape, lest she perish with Jericho, she received from the spies a most powerful "sign" of salvation, the "scarlet cord." For through the blood of Christ this whole Church is saved, in Christ himself our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen!"
Questions on the book of Kings 16

It is said of the time when Ahab reigned, "In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho; he laid its foundations in Abiram, his firstborn; and he set up its gates in Segub, his youngest son." The apparent sense is that when the above-mentioned city's builder began to lay its foundations, his firstborn, named Abiram, died; and that after the city had been built, when he tried to fortify its gates, he lost his youngest son, named Segub. Joshua predicted that this would happen when, after Jericho's destruction he made it anathema by cursing it, saying, "Cursed be the man before the Lord that shall raise up and build the city of Jericho, and in his firstborn may he lay its foundation, and in the last of his children set up its gates." Because Hiel is translated as "living for God" and Bethel as "house of God," Hiel of Bethel restores Jericho's walls (which Joshua had destroyed and cursed) whenever any who have taken up the religious life in the church resume doing the evil deeds for which the Lord Jesus forgave them on the day of [their] baptism and whenever they who have renounced the devil's pomp return to it by wanton living or prefer false doctrines or Gentile fables to the church's truth in which they were instructed.

n: Children. Achan was guilty of theft: some of the rest might have connived at his fault. He had taken what was reserved for the Lord. The offender was discovered, to inspire all with a horror for his conduct. Some of his brethren were punished, (ver. 5,) but they suffered for their own secret transgressions, or death might be no real punishment to them; while the Israelites were awakened to a sense of their own inability to conquer without the divine protection, and were forced to humble themselves. (Haydock) --- Chastisements are the marks of God's displeasure, though they frequently proceed also from his clemency. --- Achan is called Achar, 1 Paralipomenon ii. 7. These five persons occupy the space of 265 years; so that they must have been 50 or 55 years old, when they had children.

Against Hai, to see the situation and strength of that city, which was about 10 miles west, or rather north, of Jericho. It was afterwards rebuilt, 1 Esdras ii. 28. --- Bethaven and Bethel are the same place; (St. Jerome; Calmet) though many distinguish them, with Cellarius. The former name means "the house of iniquity," because Jeroboam there set up a golden calf. Bethel was its former appellation, in consequence of the vision of Jacob, Genesis xxviii.
Few. It appears, however, that the city contained 12,000 fighting men; so that these spies must have formed a false notion of its strength, chap. viii. 25.

Sabarim, which means people "broken and defeated." Septuagint, "they pursued them from the gate, till they had entirely broken them," destroying 36, and putting the rest to flight. (Calmet) --- This small disaster filled the whole camp with dismay, as the Lord generally caused the victories of his people to be complete, and without any loss, as long as they continued in his favour. None were found wanting of those who attacked and destroyed so many of the Madianites, Numbers xxxi. 49. (Haydock)

Heads. These marks of grief were very common. Achilles covered his head with ashes, tore his garments and face, when he received news of the death of his friend, Patroclus. Homer and Virgil, (Æneid xii.) speaking of Latinus, the king, says, It scissa veste Latinus---Canitiem immundo perfusam pulvere turpans.

Began. Some had established themselves in the land of Galaad. (Menochius) --- Hebrew, "would to God we had been content, and dwelt on the other side of the Jordan." Josue speaks in this animated manner, through zeal for the glory of God, (Calmet) more than for any personal inconvenience. He was grieved that any one should have merited God's displeasure. He was afraid that the Chanaanites would blaspheme the great name of the Lord, ver. 9.

Lied. Each one, on delivering up what he had taken, made profession, at least by his behaviour, (Haydock) that he retained nothing. Achan did like the rest, but he kept back of the plunder. (Calmet) --- He lied, and did not comply with the promise made by all Israel, which he was bound to observe, as much as if he had made it with his own mouth.
Sanctified. Prepared by washing, &c., to appear before the tabernacle, and to see the event. Septuagint, "purify the people." Chaldean, "call an assembly."

Find. Hebrew, "it shall be the tribe which the Lord taketh." (Haydock) --- This was done by lots, as on similar occasions, 1 Kings x. 20., and xiv. 41. When God authorized this method, there could be no danger in it. But to have recourse to lots without such authority, would be often tempting God. The apostles chose an apostle by lot: but they had first taken every precaution (Calmet) to select two persons, both fit for the important charge. (Haydock) --- To commit the choice of sacred ministers to chance would be extremely improper. "We forbid the use of lots in the elections," said Honorius. (Calmet)
Juda. The dignity of this tribe enhanced the fault of Achan. (Menochius)
My son. Clemency is the virtue of great souls. --- Give glory. Confess candidly, John ix. 24.

Garment. Hebrew, "a robe of Sannaar, or of Babylon." This city was famous for embroidered, or painted robes, such as were worn by kings, Jonas iii. 6. (Pliny, [Natural History?] viii. 48.) --- Rule, or linget. No coin was yet used. (Calmet)

His sons, &c. Probably conscious to, or accomplices of the crime of their father, (Challoner) as he could hardly have concealed these things in the midst of his tent without their knowledge. (Menochius) --- But granting, with St. Augustine (q. 8,) that they were innocent of this crime, God, who is the sovereign arbiter of life and death, might order them out of the world, on this occasion, without injustice.

Day. Hence some have drawn a very weak argument, to prove the repentance of Achan, as if he had only to undergo a temporary punishment. It is probable, however, that his sincere confession, proceeding from a penitent heart, might influence God to shew him mercy. --- Fire. Children, as well as his other effects; though some have supposed that the former were spared, as they are not here specified. Hebrew seems to include them; "and burnt them with fire after they had stoned them with stones." Chaldean says they were stoned first. (Calmet)

Achor. That is, trouble; (Challoner) in allusion to the name of Achar, as he is called in the Septuagint invariably, and in the Hebrew and Vulgate in the Book of Chronicles. (Haydock) --- This heap of stones was thrown upon the ashes of the deceased, or perhaps at his person, while he was burning at the stake, as it is the custom still among the Turks. (Roger. ii. 7.) The king of Hai was treated in this manner, chap. viii. 29. See 2 Kings xviii. 17. The vale of Achor was on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho, where a small castle, at Adommim, was built to protect travellers from the insults of robbers, who infested that part, Luke x. 30., and chap. xv. 7.

f: HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.6

But this too must not be run over idly: that when one man sinned, wrath came upon the whole people. How does this happen? When the priests, who are set over the people, wish to seem kindly toward wrongdoers, and, fearing the tongues of sinners lest perhaps they speak ill of them, forgetful of priestly severity, are unwilling to fulfill what is written: "rebuke the sinner before all, that the rest may have fear," and again: "take away the evil from among your own selves," nor, kindled with zeal for God, do they imitate the Apostle who says that "such a man is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved." Nor do they strive to fulfill that evangelical precept that, if they see one sinning, they should first meet him privately, afterward also with "two or three witnesses"; and if he shall have despised this and after the church's correction shall not have been amended, they should hold him, expelled from the church, "as a heathen and a publican." And while they spare one, they contrive the ruin of the whole church. What kind of goodness is this, what kind of mercy is it, to spare one and to bring all into danger? For the people is defiled by one sinner. Just as by one diseased sheep the whole flock is infected, so also, when one man either fornicates or commits any other kind of crime, the whole populace is defiled. And therefore let us watch over one another, and let the conduct of each one be known, especially to the priests and ministers. Nor let them think they are speaking rightly when they say: what does this concern me, if another does evil? This is to say, as the head says to the feet: what does it pertain to me, if my feet ache, if they are in a bad state? it is no concern of mine, so long as the head continues in health; or as if the eye should say to the hand: I do not need your work, what does it pertain to me if you ache, if you are wounded? shall I, the eye, be troubled by the sickness of the hand? Such, then, is what those do who preside over the churches, not considering that we who believe are all "one body," having one God, who binds us together in unity and holds us fast, namely Christ, of whose body you, who preside over the church, are the eye — for this very purpose, surely, that you may look around upon all things, survey all things, and even foresee things to come. You are a shepherd; you see the little sheep of the Lord, unaware of the danger, being carried to the precipices and hanging over the crags: do you not run to meet them? do you not call them back? do you not at least restrain them with your voice and deter them with the shout of rebuke? Are you so forgetful of the Lord's sacrament that, whereas he, "having left the ninety-nine in the heavens" for the sake of one little sheep "that had gone astray," descended to the earth and, having found it, "carried it back upon his shoulders" to heaven, we in no way at all follow the example of the master shepherd in caring for the little sheep? We do not say these things in order that anyone should be cut off for a slight fault; but if perhaps someone, having been admonished and rebuked for his offense once and again and a third time, has shown no amendment, let us use the discipline of the physician. If we have anointed with oil, if we have soothed with plasters, if we have softened with a poultice, and yet the hardness of the swelling does not yield to the medicines, the only remaining remedy is to cut it away. For so the Lord also says: "if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you." Does the hand of our body ever "cause us to stumble," or is it about this hand of the body that the Gospel says: "cut it off, and cast it away from you"? But this is what it means: that I, who seem to you to be the right hand and am named a presbyter and seem to preach the word of God, if I do anything against ecclesiastical discipline and the rule of the Gospel, so that I cause a stumbling-block to you, to the church, then the whole church, conspiring together in one consent, should cut me off as its right hand and cast me away from itself. For "it is expedient for you," the church, without me, your hand — who by doing evil "have caused a stumbling-block" — to enter into the kingdom of heaven, rather than with me "to go into hell." We have said these things for this reason, because we see it related in the holy Scriptures that on account of one man sinning "the children of Israel were made accursed," so that they were conquered by their enemies.

Behold, did not Achar the son of Zata transgress in the accursed thing, and trouble then lighted on all the congregation of Israel? And this one man was alone in his sin; but he was not alone in the death that came by his sin. And by us, too, everything of a gainful kind at this time, which is ours not in our own rightful possession, but as property strictly belonging to others, ought to be reckoned a thing devoted. For that Achar indeed took of the spoil; and those men of the present time take also of the spoil. But he took what belonged to enemies; while these now take what belongs to brethren, and aggrandize themselves with fatal gains.
HOMILIES ON EPHESIANS 6

Suppose any one should make scrutiny into all the communicants in the world, what kind of transgression is there which he would not detect? and what if he examined those in authority? Would he not find them eagerly bent upon gain? making traffic of high places? envious, malignant, vainglorious, gluttonous, and slaves to money?
Where then there is such impiety as this going on, what dreadful calamity must we not expect? And to be assured how sore vengeance they incur who are guilty of such sins as these, consider the examples of old. One single man, a common soldier, stole the sacred property, and all were smitten. Ye know, doubtless, the history I mean? I am speaking of Acham the son of Carmi, the man who stole the consecrated spoil.…
On account of all these things, let us take heed to ourselves. Do ye not see these wars? Do ye not hear of these disasters? Do ye learn no lesson from these things? Nations and whole cities are swallowed up and destroyed, and myriads as many again are enslaved to the barbarians.
If hell bring us not to our senses, yet let these things. What, are these too mere threats, are they not facts that have already taken place? Great is the punishment they have suffered, yet a greater still shall we suffer, who are not brought to our senses even by their fate.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 36: WHY WERE MEN KILLED ON ACHAR’S ACCOUNT?

IF THE SOUL THAT SINS SHALL ITSELF DIE, WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT ACHAR, THE SON OF CHARMI, SINNED, AND THIRTY MEN WERE KILLED ON HIS ACCOUNT? — Scripture spoke in a different sense from what is proposed. For it did not speak of that death which is of course common to all, but of that which is called the second death. This is what befalls sinners; but for those who died in battle, Achar’s sin was not avenged to them; rather, it harmed them by preventing them, lacking divine protection, from prevailing over their enemies. For it is not by reason of Achar that they were made weak, but because they were in no way fortified by God’s help, so that, being unable to act bravely, they were killed. Indeed, they were few against many, from which it is clear that they were overcome. There is therefore no injustice in the will of God. For He has it in His power whether He wishes to help: if He is present, He is merciful; if He is unwilling, He is just; for in such matters He is not a debtor, so as to be bound and liable. Therefore it is that Joshua, son of Nun, in distress tore his garments (ibid. 6), understanding that God had not withdrawn His help without cause.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 14: WHY WERE THIRTY-SIX MEN KILLED ON CHARMI’S ACCOUNT?

IF THE SOUL THAT SINS SHALL ITSELF DIE, HOW IS IT THAT, WHEN CHARMI SINS, THIRTY‑SIX MEN APPEAR TO HAVE BEEN KILLED ON HIS ACCOUNT? — Charmi indeed sinned, and died by stoning. But those thirty-six men who died in battle were not crushed by God, but were not helped. Through their own weakness, since they were unable to act bravely, they were killed. Therefore, on account of Charmi this came about or was hindered, because those who should have been helped were neglected by God. So, therefore, Joshua, son of Nun, in distress tore his garments, because he understood that God his helper had withdrawn His aid in this situation.
On the Duties of the Clergy 2.26.129

But human habits have so long applied themselves to this admiration of money that no one is thought worthy of honor unless he is rich. This is no new habit. No, this vice (and that makes the matter worse) grew long years ago in human hearts. When the city of Jericho fell at the sound of the priests' trumpets and Joshua the son of Nun gained the victory, he knew that the valor of the people was weakened through love of money and desire for gold. For when Achan had taken a garment of gold and two hundred shekels of silver and a golden ingot from the spoils of the ruined city, he was brought before the Lord and could not deny the theft but admitted it.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 7.7

But let us also see what his very sin was: "he stole," it says, "a tongue of gold, and placed it in his tent." I do not think that in that theft of a little gold there was such force of sin that it could stain so innumerable a church of the Lord. But let us see whether perhaps, in the inner understanding, the bitterness of this sin is so great and so grave. There is much beauty in words, and much loveliness in the discourses of the philosophers or the rhetoricians, who are all from the city of Jericho, that is, men of this world. If, then, you find among the philosophers perverse doctrines adorned with the assertions of brilliant speech, this is "the tongue of gold." But see that the splendor of the work does not deceive you, that the beauty of golden speech does not carry you away; remember that Jesus commanded all the gold that should be found in Jericho to be "accursed." If you read a poet weaving gods and goddesses in measured verses and in resplendent song, do not be delighted by the sweetness of eloquence: for it is a tongue of gold; if you take it up and place it in your tent, if you bring into your heart the things that are asserted by them, you will defile the whole church of the Lord. This the wretched Valentinus did, and Basilides; this Marcion also did. These men stole "tongues of gold" from Jericho and attempted to introduce into the churches the not-upright sects of the philosophers and to defile the whole church of the Lord. But let us follow the preceding example of the fathers; let us examine more diligently, lest anyone should have a Jerichoan "tongue" hidden in his tent, and let us cast away the evil from our very selves, because, even if we hold back, God will convict him, so that he himself will spontaneously confess and say: "I stole a tongue of gold and pure bracelets." Do you see of what sort was the theft he stole? He steals "a tongue" and "pure bracelets." Now "pure bracelets" are works in which nothing divine is mixed, but the whole is carried out according to man. Indeed, in our disputations too it is customary to say that we do not call Christ a mere man, but confess him God and man. But that which is stolen from Jericho is said to be "pure," that is, without God — which, for the one stealing it, was surely the cause of sin. And therefore let us perceive nothing pure and human concerning Christ, but let us confess him God and man alike, because the "wisdom" of God is also called "manifold," so that through these things we may deserve to take a share in "the wisdom of God," which is "Christ" Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."
Against the Pelagians 1.37

Achan sinned, and the entire nation transgressed. And the Lord said to Joshua, "The children of Israel will not be able to stand before their enemies but shall flee from their adversaries, because there is a curse in their midst. And I shall no more be with you, unless the anathema is destroyed out of you." And when they made search for the guilty person and the lot discovered him hiding, Achan, and his sons and daughters, and his asses and sheep are killed; his tent and all his possessions are destroyed by fire. Granted, that he himself committed a sin. What sin did his children commit, his oxen, his asses, his sheep? Reprehend God, why one man committed a sin and a number of people were put to death; why even he is stoned to death and all his possessions are destroyed by the avenging flame? Let us also quote the other testimony: "There was not a city," he says, "that the Lord did not deliver to the children of Israel, except the Hivites who dwell in Gibeon; they took all by fight, because it was the sentence of the Lord that their hearts should be hardened and they should fight against Israel and be killed, and that they should not deserve any clemency and should be destroyed, as the Lord commanded Moses." If it was done by the will of God that they should neither make peace with Israel nor obtain peace from Israel, let us say with the apostle: "Why then does he find fault? For who can resist his will?"
LETTER 133.9

What compulsion commands him [Paul] to do what he dislikes? And why must he not do what he wishes but what he dislikes and does not wish? He will answer you thus: "No, but, O man, who are you that replies against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, 'Why have you made me this way?' Has not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel to honor and another to dishonor?" Bring a yet graver charge against God and ask him why, when Esau and Jacob were still in the womb, he said, "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." Accuse him of injustice because, when Achan the son of Carmi stole part of the spoil of Jericho, he butchered so many thousands for the fault of one.

n: Men. Masius and Salien (Haydock) suppose that Josue selected out of them 30,000; 5000 of whom were to be placed in ambush, and the rest were to pretend that they were terrified at the approach of the king of Hai, and to flee with Josue. But the text seems to assert that all accompanied their general, (Calmet) excepting such as were left to guard the camp. (Haydock)

King. There was this difference, that the king of Hai was to be gibbeted, and his corpse stoned, while the city was to be plundered by the Israelites. --- It. This mode of warfare is equally just, as if the enemy was attacked in the open field. Dolus an virtus quis in hoste requirat? (Virgil) --- God was pleased to authorize it on this occasion, that his people might be less exposed, being under some apprehensions on account of the former defeat. Some nations have preferred to encounter the enemy openly. (Grotius, Jur. iii. 1, 20.) But their example is no law for others. "When the war is just, it matters not whether a person gain the victory by open fighting or by stratagem." (St. Augustine, q. 10.) "It is often prudent to conceal the truth." (contra Mend. x.) People engaged in warfare, allow each other to take such advantages. God could easily have routed these few men by means of the army of Israel, or by a miracle, as he did at Jericho. (Haydock) --- But he is at liberty to act as he thinks proper. The ambush was laid on the south-west side of Hai, so that those of Bethel might not perceive it, as they came out to the assistance of their countrymen, ver. 17. Five thousand were placed in one place, and 25,000 in another, while the main body of the army, under Josue, took a circuit by the east, and came to attack the city on the north side. (Calmet)
Ready to enter the city, when its soldiers are all in pursuit of us. (Haydock)
And turn, &c. Josue had not fled before. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "against us, as at the first, we will flee before them."
Fire. They were to set some houses on fire for a signal, but the whole city was not to be destroyed (Calmet) till the Israelites had collected the plunder. (Haydock)
Ancients, who had a command in the army, and assisted Josue with their counsel. They gave him an account of the state and numbers of the army. (Calmet)

Five thousand. These were part of the 30,000 mentioned above, ver. 3 . (Challoner) --- Josue had given orders to have them placed in ambush apart; (Calmet) unless, perhaps, he places these himself in some secret place. (Haydock)
Night. He spent the forepart of it at Galgal, to prevent any suspicion, ver. 9. But setting out very early, (ver. 10,) he arrived at Hai before sun-rise.
Desert of Bethel, fit only for pasturage, chap. xviii. 12.
Afraid. Hebrew, "made as if they were beaten before them, and fled." Thus they drew on the king of Hai, so as to leave the ambush in his rear. (Calmet)

Not one fit to bear arms. (Worthington) --- Bethel. As soon as the people of this city perceived the Israelites fleeing, they rushed out to assist the king of Hai in the pursuit. But when they saw the former rally, before they had joined their friends, (Calmet) they very prudently retired, and left the unhappy citizens of Hai to their fate. (Haydock) --- Hence all who were slain belonged to the latter city, ver. 25.

Shield, as Moses lifted up his hands, Exodus xvii. 11. Some translate, "dart, spear," or "sword." (Septuagint; Ecclesiasticus xvi. 3.) (Calmet) --- The buckler might be suspended on a spear, (Menochius) that it might be seen afar off (Worthington) by some appointed to keep watch on purpose. (Haydock)

Josue. This king was reserved for greater torments and ignominy. It was the ancient custom to present kings and chief commanders to the victorious general, who rewarded those who brought them. (Grotius)
For ever, or for a long time. It was rebuilt before the captivity, 2 Esdras vii. 31.
Gibbet. Septuagint, "a cross." Some say that the king was first killed; but that assertion is destitute of proof. The corpse was taken down before night, Deuteronomy xxi. 22.

Hebal. The Samaritan Chronicle says, on Mount Garizim. No doubt Josue complied with the injunctions of Moses: but we have seen that there are reasons to doubt which mountain he pitched upon, Deuteronomy xxvii. 4. (Haydock) --- It seems more probable that the altar would be upon Garizim, where the blessings were proclaimed, if the texts of Moses and of Josue did not formally assert the contrary. (Calmet) --- But if they have been interpolated, nothing certain can be deduced from those passages. Josephus ([Antiquities?] iv. 8,) says that the altar was between the two mountains, not far from Sichem, which was built at the foot of Garizim; and it is not probable that this historian, the mortal enemy of the Samaritans, would have hesitated to assert that the altar was upon Hebal, if the texts had been so positive, in his time. It is undeniable that the tribes of Levi, and of Ephraim, were upon Garizim; and consequently Josue and the priests must have been there; and who would then officiate at the altar on Hebal? See Kennicott, who ably refutes the insinuations of the infidel, Collins, against the character of the Samaritans. When this altar was erected the learned are not agreed. (Haydock) --- Some say, immediately after the passage of the Jordan, and that the 12 stones taken from the bed of the river, were used for that purpose. Josephus says five years elapsed, and R. Ismael supposes that the altar was not built during the 14 years after the passage of the Jordan. But it is most probable that Josue complied with the command of God as soon as he had procured a sort of peace, (Haydock) by the conquest of these two cities, and was thus enabled to penetrate into the heart of the country, where Garizim was situated, not in the plain of Jericho, as Eusebius imagined, but near Sichem, (Calmet) about 30 or 40 miles to the north-west of Jericho. (Haydock)

Iron. Spencer complains that the Protestants have not translated barzel, "iron tool," as [in] Deuteronomy xxvii. 5. This translation is found in their more ancient editions of 1537-49, &c. (Kennicott) --- But the difference is very unimportant. The reason of this prohibition is given, Exodus xx. 25. --- He offered; so we read that he wrote, blessed and cursed, &c., because these things were done at least by his authority. It is not necessary to suppose that he engraved the words of the law with his own hands, or that he passed from Garizim, where he had been pronouncing the blessings, to Hebal, in order to denounce the curses. (Haydock) --- He probably commissioned some of the princes on Hebal to perform the office of cursing, after he had repeated the blessings himself from Garizim; and the select company of Levites before the ark, having answered or repeated the words, the whole multitude stationed at the foot of each mountain, testified their entire approbation by shouting Amen; the six tribes near Garizim thus ratifying the blessings; and the rest, at the foot of Hebal, giving their consent that the transgressors should be cursed. (Kennicott) --- Hence Josue must have sacrificed by the hands of the priests. (Haydock) --- Various instances are produced to shew that princes and prophets have, on extraordinary occasions, performed this office themselves, 1 Kings vi. 15., and vii. 9., and 3 Kings xviii. 32. (Calmet) --- But these must have either received a dispensation from God, or they must have employed the ministry of the legal priests; or, in fine, their actions, like that of Saul, (1 Kings xiii. 9,) of Absalom, (1 Kings i. 9,) Herod, &c., may have been deserving of blame. (Haydock) --- The Jews assert that in the desert no one was permitted to sacrifice, except in the tabernacle; but that this prohibition ceased at Galgal, as the ark had no fixed abode, and thus Josue might offer sacrifice himself. Afterwards the law was enforced, while the ark was at Silo. But upon its being removed to Nobe, Maspha, and Gabaon, people resumed their former liberty; and hence there was nothing to hinder Samuel, Saul, and David from offering sacrifice, till the temple was erected. (Outram de Sac. i. 2; Grotius in Deuteronomy xii. 8.) This sacred office was formerly exercised by kings, particularly at Athens, where, after the people became more numerous, Theseus appointed the king of sacrifices to keep up the memory of the ancient practice. (Demost. c. Neream.) (Calmet) --- The like was done at Rome under the republic. (Haydock)

Stones, of which the altar was formed, (Calmet) or on a separate monument, (Masius) consisting of two stones of black marble, so as to leave the letters prominent, and to fill up the vacuities with white plaster, that they might be seen more plainly, and might, at the same time, be more durable than if they had been only written on the cement, whatever some may have said of the tenacity of the ancient plaster. --- Deuteronomy. &c., or copy of the Decalogue, which, by way of eminence, is called the law, Acts vii. 53. It is distinguished from the blessings and the curses; (ver. 34,) and Moses referred to it, as already existing, (Deuteronomy xxvii. 3, 8,) though the Book of Deuteronomy was not finished till afterwards. He might point to the very tables contained in the ark. "This law, consisting of only 16 verses, might easily be engraved on this solemn day; whereas to engrave the 80 verses of blessings and cursings, would be improbable; and engraving the Pentateuch, or indeed the Book of Deuteronomy, had been impossible." That the Decalogue was to be thus solemnly proclaimed is evident, from the Samaritan text, Exodus xx. 18. (Kennicott) --- This was the covenant which God had made with his people, (Deuteronomy iv. 13,) and which Moses cautions the Israelites to observe; as upon their fidelity, their present and future happiness entirely depended. It was on this title alone that they could hold the land of Chanaan; and therefore Josue takes care thus publicly to admonish them of their duty. (Haydock) --- The Rabbins say that the whole Pentateuch was written on this occasion in 70 languages, that no nation might plead ignorance. But we can hardly believe that even the Book of Deuteronomy could be written, and read, and explained to the people, as that would require many days. (Calmet)

Hebal. "Gerizim and Ebal, says Maundrell, p. 59, are separated by a narrow valley, not above a furlong broad; and Naplosa, (the ancient Sychem) consisting chiefly of two streets lying parallel, is built at the foot of, and under Gerizim." The princes, representing the different tribes, were stationed on these mountains, and the crowd at the foot of them, while a select company of Levites attended the ark in the midst, and repeated what the princes proclaimed, that the multitude might answer Amen, as they turned successively to them; (Kennicott) or the princes might answer Amen, from the top of the two hills. (Calmet) --- And first. Protestants, "as Moses....had commanded before, that they should bless the people of Israel." But if Josue blessed them himself, (Haydock) all superiors might do so, as parents bless their children. (Worthington)
Words. Hebrew, "words of the law, the blessings," &c. (Haydock)

Repeated. Coverdale's Bible has "Josua caused it to be proclaimed." "It is very common in Scripture to represent a person as doing that which is done by another, in his name and by his authority." (Kennicott) --- Josue might be in the midst to preside, (Calmet) or rather he would be along with the princes of the six tribes on Mount Garizim, ver. 30. (Haydock) --- Thus the covenant entered into between God and the Israelites, was solemnly ratified when the latter first entered the promised land. The greatest part of those who had been present at Horeb had perished in the wilderness. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.2

When these things have been heard, it is likely that the hearers will say: what is this to me? What does it profit me if I come to know that those who inhabited Ai were conquered, as though similar or even more powerful wars had not been waged or are not being waged? Was this the care of the Holy Spirit, that, leaving aside the destructions of so many and so great and noble cities, the battle of the city of Ai should be written and consigned to the sacred volumes? Perhaps what we are doing is rash, in that we attempt to explain places of Holy Scripture so lofty and so difficult; but if you aid us with your prayers, we shall not only escape the fault of audacity, but also God the Father of the Word, embracing our devotion, "will give a word for the opening of our mouth," whereby both you may be edified and we may appear not undevout. Praying, therefore, and attentive in mind, listen. First, because of our sins we were conquered, and those who inhabited Ai slew a great many of us. Ai is interpreted "Chaos." But we know that Chaos is the place or dwelling of the contrary powers, whose king and prince is the devil. Coming against him, Jesus divides the people into two parts, and some indeed he stations in the front, others in the rear, who may come unexpectedly upon the backs of the enemy. And see whether that is not the first part of the people, of which he says: "I have not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and of which the Apostle says: "but grace and peace to every man who works good, to the Jew first, then also to the Greek," that is, to the Gentile who comes after. This, then, is the people who is stationed in front and, as it were, flees with Jesus. But the latter people is the one which is gathered from the nations, and which, coming unexpectedly — for who would have hoped that the nations would be saved? — cuts down the adversaries the more fiercely from behind; and thus each people lays low and conquers the throng of demons enclosed in the middle.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.1

We entreat you, O hearers of the sacred volumes, not to listen with weariness or distaste to the things that are read, on the ground that their narrative seems to be less delightful. For you ought to know that the things which are read are indeed worthy of the utterance of the Holy Spirit, but for explaining them we have need of that grace of the Holy Spirit of which the Apostle speaks: "to one, moreover, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit." We too, then, have need of these things in the present passages, in which it is related that Jesus succeeded Moses, and that he himself leads the people, and a certain such history is prefigured in the present reading. Those who inhabited the city of Ai at first seemed indeed to conquer and to turn back the sons of Israel because of the sin which they had committed. But afterward, when the evil had been removed from their midst, Jesus, the leader of the people, is commanded by God to divide the people into two parts, so that one part should feign flight, while the other part should lie waiting in ambush, by which Ai might be deceived when Jesus should give the command. When these things had been thus arranged, "the king of Ai, seeing" Jesus and the sons of Israel from afar, "is stirred up against them into battle." And when the former feigned flight, the others pursue them the more fiercely, and, as though about to carry off spoils from the enemy, all together "go forth out of the city," so that, as Scripture says, "they left the city empty." But after they had advanced to the appointed place, Jesus turned and gave a signal that "those who were in the ambushes should rise up" and cut down the backs of the enemy; and thus those who were last and these who were first slay all the enemy enclosed in the middle. And in this manner, when those who inhabited Ai had been conquered, "they hanged" their "king upon a double wood."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.2

But perhaps you may say to me: how, then, is the former people set as though fleeing? And quite consistently. For those who follow Jesus were seen to flee from the legal burdens and precepts, from the observance of the sabbath, from the circumcision of the flesh, from the slaughter of victims. But again he who has followed Christ, the perfection and fullness of the law, does not flee.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.6

But something else also occurs to me as I consider in this place "Jesus fleeing from the face" of the army of Ai. What do you think it is that "Jesus fleeing" signified? Let us see whether perhaps there is something which we conquer by fleeing, and there is some perfect virtue in flight. Paul the Apostle teaches us, saying: "flee fornication." You see, then, that there is a certain "spirit of fornication," which we ought to flee, whoever of us wishes to remain chastely and piously and modestly in Christ. This flight, then, is the one which has salvation; this flight is of virtue; this flight confers blessedness. And not only is the spirit of fornication to be fled, but in like manner, just as it was said, "flee fornication," let us hear it said to us: flee anger, flee avarice, flee envy and spite, flee detractions and evil-speakings. And yet I know not whether anyone escapes these, I know not whether anyone gets away. Such was that army of Ai, which Jesus taught his soldiers to flee, and concerning these perhaps he commands his disciples, saying: "if they persecute you in this city, flee into another; and if in another, flee into another." For he wishes us to flee from enemies of this kind, he wishes us to be made far from evils of this kind; and if in the meanwhile we can escape the contagions of these evils by fleeing, then, seeing the devotion and the purpose of our mind, certain holy virtues — those perhaps of which the Apostle Paul says: "are they not all ministering spirits sent forth into ministry for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?" — who perhaps are the holy angels, who, seeing us suffer the pursuit of the demons, rise up against those who pursue us and, cutting them all down from behind, slay them. For Jesus is with those who suffer pursuit, rather than with those who persecute. And rightly, because Jesus delights to be with those who "flee fornication," who flee pride, who flee deceit, and who flee falsehood. If, then, we thus understand the things which are written, the reading will perhaps seem worthy of the pen of the Holy Spirit. For what does it profit me if I know that "the king of Ai was hanged upon a double wood"? But if I know that the virtue of the cross is twofold, on which both Christ is hanged in the flesh and the devil with his army is triumphed over, from the understanding of the sacrament my soul will be edified. And still more perhaps, that we may extend the breadth of the mystery yet more loftily, in this wood is understood to be "the knowledge of good and evil," on which both the good Christ and the evil devil hung, but the evil one indeed that he might perish, and the good one that he might live from power; as the Apostle also says concerning Christ, that "even if he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God." Nay, not only that he might live, but that he might give life, because he is "the last Adam unto a life-giving spirit." But these things must be understood to be said figuratively; for Christ himself is called "the tree of life." But just as in other passages he is shown to be both priest and victim and altar, and the one meaning is not hindered by the other, but each single thing is understood figuratively concerning him in its own places, so also now in the figures of the sacraments the diversity of persons taken up concerning one and the same thing will not hinder.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.7

But let us see what is also written in what follows: "and they struck them," he says, "with the edge of the sword, until there was not left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape." When the Jews read these things, they become cruel and thirst for human blood, thinking that the saints too struck those who inhabited Ai, so that "there should not be left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape," not understanding that in these words mysteries are foreshadowed, and that this is rather indicated to us, that of these whose dwelling is chaos and who reigned in the abyss, of the demons, we ought to leave none at all, but to slay them all. But we slay the demons not by destroying their very substance; but because their work and their zeal is this, to make men sin, and this is their life, if we sin, without doubt it is their destruction, if we do not sin. Therefore the saints slay the inhabitants of Ai and destroy them and do not let go one of them — those, without doubt, who with all diligence guard their heart, lest "evil thoughts proceed" from it; but also those who watch over their mouth, so that "every evil word may not proceed from" their "mouth": this is "to leave none who might escape," when no evil word escapes them either. Come, then, you too, let us prepare ourselves for battles of this kind, let us strike Ai "with the edge of the sword" and extinguish all who inhabit chaos, all the contrary powers. Would that I too, even now, while I speak the word of God to you, might be able to strike the heart of the sinner! For if I do so, it is certain that with the "sword of my mouth" I shall strike fornication, I shall strike malice, I shall repress fury and, if there are any other evils, "with the edge of the sword," that is, with the speech of my mouth, I shall quench them and "shall not leave of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape." For if we extinguish all these enemies of ours, then we shall truly celebrate a feast day to God and, our adversaries being vanquished, we shall rejoice with glad solemnity. Some such thing seems to me to be signified also by the holy prophet in the psalms, where he says of himself that "in the mornings I slew all the sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity." For whether "the city of the Lord" is taken to be the church of the living God, the teachers cast out from the church and slay those "who work iniquity," the contrary demons and the adversary powers, who compel men to sin by teaching, by instructing, and by unlocking the mysteries hidden in the divine letters from such places as those in which we now are; or whether by "the city of the Lord" we understand the soul of each one of us, which is built by the Lord from "living stones," that is, from various and diverse virtues: from that city too every holy and diligent man casts out "the sinners," that is, "slays in the morning" the worst thoughts and depraved desires. For the just man says: "in the mornings I meditated on you, because you were my helper." What is this "morning," except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is "the true light" and "rising in our hearts" and illuminating the darkness of our ignorance and revealing to us mysteries of this kind, makes us "see light in his light"? If ever, then, you read in the holy scriptures of the battles of the just, the slaughters and the massacres of the slain, and that the saints spare none at all of the enemy — nay rather, that even if they had spared, "it is reckoned to them as sin," just as "it was reckoned" to Saul, who "had preserved alive Agag king of Amalek" — understand the wars of the just in this manner in which we have expounded above, because these wars are waged by them against sin. But how will the just remain, if they have reserved even some little of sin in themselves? And therefore it is said of these that "they left not even one who might be saved or escape." Perhaps you may not believe me that a battle is enjoined upon us against sin; believe Paul, who says: "you have not yet resisted unto blood against sin." You see that a battle "against sin" is set before you, and that this fight is to be consummated "unto the shedding of blood"? Or does not the divine Scripture indicate these things evidently, in those places too where it is its custom to say: "sanctify a war" and: "you shall fight the fight of the Lord"? For what else is it "to sanctify a war," except, when all the enemies of our soul, which are the vices of sins, have been slain, and "the members which are upon the earth having been mortified" and all evil desires cut off, to be made "holy in body and spirit" and, acting bravely, to come to the sight of the living God and to be crowned by Christ Jesus our Lord for the palm of the victory of virtue by merit? "To whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 8.5

But let us see what follows in the sequel: "and Jesus burned Ai," he says, "and it was made a wasteland, that it should not be inhabited forever." You see that these things which follow pertain more to the truth of the mystery than of the history. For that place of earth is not so much uninhabitable forever as the place of the demons will then be uninhabitable, when now no one will sin, "neither will sin reign" in anyone, when the devil and his angels will be delivered to eternal fire, our Lord Jesus Christ sitting as king and judge and saying to those who conquered, both the first and the last: "come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you by my Father."
