The "Canaanites" too were named, and those also were named who are "over against the face of Egypt," and those who are "from the borders of Ekron" and from the left parts of the rivers, and very many other nations; and concerning the Sidonians alone the Lord says that he "will overthrow" them. Now the "Sidonians," as we have already said before, are interpreted as hunters. Who then are understood to be these evil hunters, whom the Lord "exterminates," if not those adverse powers, concerning whom the prophet says that "they have prepared snares for my feet"? — with which, namely, they hunt and entrap souls unto sin. These, then, the Lord "exterminates"; for if such hunters as these shall have perished, when there is no longer anyone to "stretch out snares" and nets to entrap souls in sin, then "each one shall rest under his own vine and under his own fig tree."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 16.5

But that also was read to us today, that Moses gave an inheritance to certain men; and after these things it is read that Jesus too, according to the precept of the Lord, distributed the inheritance. First, then, Moses distributed the inheritance, but second Jesus. Now understand Moses as the law. These, then, who lived according to the law received the inheritance first, but outside the land of promise. Then afterward, when they had received the land of inheritance, they do not possess it nor divide it among themselves, but they wait until it is distributed to them by lot through Jesus. Is not this evidently what the Apostle says to the Hebrews, writing about the "former fathers," whom he said "pleased God by faith"? And he added, saying: "but all these, having obtained testimony through faith, did not yet receive the promises, God providing something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us." They have therefore already their "promise" and have found rest, and have been judged worthy through Moses to take the inheritance; nevertheless they too still fight and are in the contest on behalf of those who serve as soldiers under Jesus. But you ask who these are that fight, and what is that fight which they wage. I judge it thus, that all those "fathers" who "fell asleep" before us fight together with us and help us by their prayers. For so also I heard a certain one of the elder teachers saying, in that place where it is written in Numbers that: "that synagogue shall lick up this synagogue, as a calf licks up the green grass of the field." He said: why was a likeness of this kind taken up, unless because this is what is to be understood in the passage — that the "synagogue" of the Lord, which has gone before us among the saints, shall with mouth and tongue consume the adversary synagogue, that is, shall consume our adversaries with prayers and supplications? Not therefore with arms are we to fight against our invisible enemies, but with prayers and meditations on the word of God and with right works and right thoughts. For so also the fathers were armed, conquering by faith and by works. See, finally, that it is so written of them: "they believed," it says, "God and Moses his servant"; and "then Moses sang this song" and said: "let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored." So then let us too, cultivating full faith and perfect works, unceasing prayers, meditation on the divine word, spiritual understanding, and fortified in all these as with the arms of God, "let us stand against the wiles of the devil," calling upon God our helper in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 17.2

Nevertheless, let us see what it is that is described through the shadow, since in the shadow of the law the truth is outlined. There is reported, then, a first and a second division of the inheritance that was made — the first indeed through Moses, but the second, which is also the more powerful, is described as made through Jesus. And "Moses" decrees a possession "beyond the Jordan to the tribe of Reuben and to the tribe of Gad and to the half tribe of Manasseh," but all the rest receive their inheritance through Jesus. We have already spoken about these matters before — how those who "had pleased God" through the law, going before in time those who through faith in Jesus arrive at the things promised, do not yet obtain the things that are perfect, awaiting those who, later indeed in a different time but by one faith, will please God, as the Apostle says: "that they should not be made perfect without us." Meanwhile, neither Moses nor Jesus gave the Levites an inheritance, because "the Lord God himself is their inheritance." And in this matter what else is to be understood, except that there are in the Church of the Lord certain ones who by the virtue of their soul and the grace of their merits go before all the rest, of whom "the Lord himself" is said to be their "inheritance"? And if it is permitted to venture in such matters and to open up something of a hidden secret, let us see whether perhaps this is what the figure of the priests or the Levites secretly shows — that in the whole people (I mean of those who are saved) the greater and by far the more numerous part is without doubt of those who, simply believing in the fear of God, through good works, through honorable morals and commendable deeds, "please the Lord"; but few there are, and very rare, who, giving their effort to wisdom and knowledge and keeping their mind clean and pure and cultivating their souls with all illustrious virtues, illuminate for the rest of the simpler ones, through the grace of teaching, the road on which they walk and come to salvation. These perhaps are now designated under the name of the Levites and the priests, whose "inheritance is the Lord himself," who is the "wisdom" which they loved above all others. I find, however, a certain difference in the things which Moses distributed and in those which Jesus distributed. For Moses, "distributing the land beyond the Jordan to the two and a half tribes," did not give the Levites the portion of a dwelling that fell to them; but Jesus gave it not only in those tribes which he himself apportions, but also in those which had been settled by Moses beyond the Jordan. For dwellings are decreed for the Levites in each single tribe, so that through this we might recognize a much more magnificent mystery. For this Levitical or priestly order, which devotes its effort to the wisdom and knowledge of God, could not receive from Moses a lot of habitation, because Moses was not a minister of the truth, but "of the shadow and the copy." But Jesus our Lord, who was "the Wisdom of God," himself provides dwellings for the wise. For Moses could not say: "Go, sell all your things which you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me" — for this is to give a portion to the Levites — nor could Moses say: "Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple," nor could Moses say: "Everyone who does not hate father or mother and brothers and sisters and children, and moreover even his own soul, cannot be my disciple." This Moses could not say, and therefore he himself could not apportion the dwellings of the priests and Levites. Blessed, therefore, is he who shows himself to be such and is found to be perfect in all these things which Jesus commanded, so that from Jesus he may receive the lot of a heavenly dwelling in the world to come; of whom the Lord Jesus himself says: "Father, I will that where I am, these also may be with me," and: "as I in you and you in me are one, that these also may be one in us."

n: Princes, whose names are given, Numbers xxxiv. 17. There were 12, including Josue and Eleazar. The tribes of Ruben and Gad sent none of their princes, as they were not concerned in this distribution.

Tribe. God regulated the lots, as he had authorized Jacob and Moses to foretell how the country should be divided. By this method, he precluded every pretence of discontent among the tribes. Each of them drew a ticket, on which a certain portion of land was described; or perhaps in one urn the names of the tribes, and in another the lands were specified, (Calmet) and the tickets were drawn by two persons of irreproachable character, probably by Eleazar and Josue. (Haydock) (Numbers xxvi. 54.) --- Only the tribes of Juda and of Joseph received their portions at Galgal, chap. xviii.

Suburbs. A certain quantity of ground, which the Levites were not allowed to till or plant with vines. (Grotius) (Numbers xxxv. 4.) --- The tribe of Manasses, which was divided, fell heir to the portion which would have been allotted to Levi, who was also scattered among his brethren. (Haydock) --- Thus Joseph obtained the birth-right of Ruben. (Calmet) --- Twelve portions were made, as Jacob had adopted Ephraim and Manasses, Genesis xlviii. (Worthington)
Land: or they were making all necessary preparations for the work, when Caleb came to remind Josue of what had been promised to him. No doubt land-measurers would be sent through the country.

Jephone was the father of Caleb. Esron and Cenez probably some of his ancestors, 1 Paralipomenon ii. 18., and Numbers xxxiii. 12. What Caleb here asserts, must have been delivered by word of mouth, in the hearing of the people, Deuteronomy i. 36. Moses declared not that Caleb was to have the whole country but that he should enter into it, and possess the environs of Hebron. (Calmet)
March. Hebrew, "to enter and to go out." Septuagint add, "to war."

Me. He trusts not in his own strength, but in the assistance of God, which he modestly acknowledges is not due to him. (Calmet) --- God's promises are indeed sure on his part; but being conditional, and the will of man being free, he adds perhaps. (Worthington)

Blessed him, wishing him all success. --- Gave him. Some think that Josue himself attacked the giants of that country with all the forces, as it is mentioned by anticipation, chap. x. 28. But there seems to be no need of this, as Caleb might attack them a second time with his own family and the assistance of the tribe of Juda, after they had seized those places again, while Josue was in the north. Hebron was granted to him without drawing lots. When he was besieging Cariath Sepher, he promised his daughter to the person who should first enter; and Othoniel, his brother, or nephew, obtained her in marriage, chap. xv. 17., and Judges i. 10. It seems, therefore, that this family carried on this war, as the Fabii did at Rome, without the interference of the commonwealth, though Grotius asserts the contrary. (Calmet)

Hebron belonged, &c. All the country thereabouts, depending on Hebron, was given to Caleb; but the city itself, with the suburbs, was one of those that were given to the priests to dwell in. (Challoner) --- Caleb might also dwell, (Calmet) and be lord of the city, (Salien) though the profits (Haydock) or the town belonged to the priests, chap. xxi. 11. (Worthington)

Cariath Arbe, "the city of Arbe," and ancient giant; or "of four," which the Jews explain of four great patriarchs, who were buried there. --- Adam, &c. St. Jerome seems to favour the opinion that Adam was one of these, whose tomb ennobled Hebron, though many of the Fathers think he was buried on Mount Calvary. Others think that his body, or skull at least, was translated thither. But we cannot depend on any of these traditions. Most commentators explain the Hebrew, "The ancient name of Hebron with Cariath Arbe; (Calmet) he was a man great among the Enacim." (Haydock) --- Adam is often put for a man in general, 2 Kings vii. 19., and Osee xi. 4. (Calmet; Amama) --- Septuagint, "the city of Arbo. This was the metropolis of the Enacim." (Haydock) --- Wars, for a time, particularly from such wars as engaged the attention of all Israel. The different tribes had to encounter and drive out the Chanaanites who might be left in their respective districts. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 18.1

Let us learn from the law, which describes for us of necessity the division of the land, said to have been made first through Moses and secondly also through Jesus — not that we should keep both, but that, learning the meaning of each, we may hold only that one which is handed down by Jesus our Lord. Now that land which is "beyond the Jordan" Moses distributed; but this one, which is the "holy land" and the "good land," "Jesus and the princes of the tribes of Israel" distributed. You see, then, that when that true inheritance of the "holy land" begins to be distributed by the Savior, the "princes of the tribes" also of the true and spiritual "Israel" will be taken up. And whom do we suppose to be the "princes" of our tribes, or the princes of the church, if not the holy Apostles, to whom the Savior says: "you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel"? Yet there is taken up for the division a priest as well, who is the hidden and mystical word of God; for so it says that "Jesus and Eleazar" came together to divide the land.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 17.1

Just as those who receive the law — which is a "shadow" of that true law — serve "the shadow and copy of the heavenly things," so those who divide the inheritance of the land in Judaea follow "the copy and shadow" of the heavenly division. The truth, therefore, was in the heavens, but the "shadow and copy" of the truth was on the earth. And so long as this "shadow" stood firm on the earth, there was an earthly Jerusalem, there was a temple, there was an altar, there was also a visible cult, there were high priests and priests, there stood also the cities and villages of Judaea and all these things which are now recited as described in this book. But when, at the coming of our Savior, God descending from the heavens, "the truth arose from the earth, and righteousness looked down from heaven," the "shadow and copies" fell. For Jerusalem fell, the temple fell, the altar was taken away, so that now there is no place, either "on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem," where one ought to worship, but "the true worshippers, who worship the Father, worship in spirit and in truth." Thus, then, when the truth was present, "the type and shadow" ceased; and when that temple was present, which was fashioned in the womb of the virgin by "the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High," the temple built of stones was demolished. The high priest "of the good things to come" was present, and the high priests "of bulls and goats" ceased. "The Lamb of God came, who takes away the sin of the world," and the lamb taken from the flocks and slaughtered to no purpose through so many ages came to an end. Therefore, if all these things which had been given to the men of former times in a shadow ceased when the truth was present and standing by, it followed without doubt that, once the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven had been laid open, the earthly inheritance too should cease. And the reason why all these things should come to an end is this: "that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world become subject to God," lest perhaps some from the unbelieving people should take occasions for their unbelief and, holding the "shadows" handed down to them from ancient times — whether of the temple or the altar or the high priests or the priests — should seem to themselves, while the state of the ancient cult remained, to be transgressing the order of religion if they should pass over to the faith. For this reason, then, divine providence arranged that all these things which had of old been foreshadowed on the earth should be taken away, so that with the types ceasing they might in a certain way find a way of seeking the truth. If therefore, O Jew, coming to the earthly city Jerusalem you find it overthrown and reduced to ashes and cinders, do not weep, as you now do like "children in your understanding"; do not lament, but instead of the earthly one seek the heavenly. Look upward, and there you will find "the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of all." If you see the altar abandoned, I do not wish you to be grieved; if you do not find a high priest, I do not wish you to despair: there is an altar in the heavens, and beside it stands the high priest "of the good things to come," "chosen by God according to the order of Melchizedech." Thus, then, by the piety and mercy of God even the earthly inheritance has been taken away from you, so that you may seek an inheritance in the heavens.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 17.2

Nevertheless, let us see what it is that is described through the shadow, since in the shadow of the law the truth is outlined. There is reported, then, a first and a second division of the inheritance that was made — the first indeed through Moses, but the second, which is also the more powerful, is described as made through Jesus. And "Moses" decrees a possession "beyond the Jordan to the tribe of Reuben and to the tribe of Gad and to the half tribe of Manasseh," but all the rest receive their inheritance through Jesus. We have already spoken about these matters before — how those who "had pleased God" through the law, going before in time those who through faith in Jesus arrive at the things promised, do not yet obtain the things that are perfect, awaiting those who, later indeed in a different time but by one faith, will please God, as the Apostle says: "that they should not be made perfect without us." Meanwhile, neither Moses nor Jesus gave the Levites an inheritance, because "the Lord God himself is their inheritance." And in this matter what else is to be understood, except that there are in the Church of the Lord certain ones who by the virtue of their soul and the grace of their merits go before all the rest, of whom "the Lord himself" is said to be their "inheritance"? And if it is permitted to venture in such matters and to open up something of a hidden secret, let us see whether perhaps this is what the figure of the priests or the Levites secretly shows — that in the whole people (I mean of those who are saved) the greater and by far the more numerous part is without doubt of those who, simply believing in the fear of God, through good works, through honorable morals and commendable deeds, "please the Lord"; but few there are, and very rare, who, giving their effort to wisdom and knowledge and keeping their mind clean and pure and cultivating their souls with all illustrious virtues, illuminate for the rest of the simpler ones, through the grace of teaching, the road on which they walk and come to salvation. These perhaps are now designated under the name of the Levites and the priests, whose "inheritance is the Lord himself," who is the "wisdom" which they loved above all others. I find, however, a certain difference in the things which Moses distributed and in those which Jesus distributed. For Moses, "distributing the land beyond the Jordan to the two and a half tribes," did not give the Levites the portion of a dwelling that fell to them; but Jesus gave it not only in those tribes which he himself apportions, but also in those which had been settled by Moses beyond the Jordan. For dwellings are decreed for the Levites in each single tribe, so that through this we might recognize a much more magnificent mystery. For this Levitical or priestly order, which devotes its effort to the wisdom and knowledge of God, could not receive from Moses a lot of habitation, because Moses was not a minister of the truth, but "of the shadow and the copy." But Jesus our Lord, who was "the Wisdom of God," himself provides dwellings for the wise. For Moses could not say: "Go, sell all your things which you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me" — for this is to give a portion to the Levites — nor could Moses say: "Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple," nor could Moses say: "Everyone who does not hate father or mother and brothers and sisters and children, and moreover even his own soul, cannot be my disciple." This Moses could not say, and therefore he himself could not apportion the dwellings of the priests and Levites. Blessed, therefore, is he who shows himself to be such and is found to be perfect in all these things which Jesus commanded, so that from Jesus he may receive the lot of a heavenly dwelling in the world to come; of whom the Lord Jesus himself says: "Father, I will that where I am, these also may be with me," and: "as I in you and you in me are one, that these also may be one in us."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 17.3

But if, hearing that the inheritance of the perfect and the more eminent is called the Lord, you are ignorant and in doubt as to what that is which is designated under this name, hear that "the Lord is wisdom." He, therefore, to whom the Lord is said to be his inheritance, this one will take the inheritance of wisdom. The Lord is called "righteousness." He, therefore, whose inheritance is the Lord, this one will obtain the inheritance of righteousness. The Lord is "peace," the Lord is "redemption," the Lord is "salvation," in the Lord are "the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden." All these things he will receive in his inheritance, whose inheritance the Lord shall have been. Nevertheless, even these, to whom the "wisdom" of God and the "Word" of God and "truth" and "righteousness" is said to be their inheritance, meanwhile receive their dwelling together with those whose inheritance is held on the earth, so that from fellowship with them those who by themselves are not yet able may through them be made partakers of the "wisdom and knowledge" of God and of his "truth" and "Word." And thus the divine dispensation extends even to the very least, so that those who cannot in the first place exist as capable of divine grace may deserve to be illuminated from fellowship with these, and that may be fulfilled which is written: "he who had much did not abound; and he who had least was not diminished," but also that which the Apostle says to the Corinthians concerning the saints of Jerusalem: "that your abundance," he says, "may make up for their want, and their abundance may make up for your want." So therefore now too the Levite and the priest, who do not have land, are commanded to dwell together with the Israelite who has land, so that the priest and the Levite may receive from the Israelite the earthly things which they do not have, and again the Israelite may receive from the priest and the Levite the heavenly and divine things which he does not have. For the law of God has been committed to the priests and the Levites, that they may give their effort to this alone and be free for the word of God without any anxiety. But again, in order that they may be able to be free, they must make use of the ministries of the laity. For if the layman does not provide the things which are necessary to the priests and the Levites, they, being occupied in such things — that is, in bodily cares — will be less free for the law of God; and while they are not free and not giving their effort to the law of God, you are endangered. For the light of knowledge which is in them will be darkened, since you do not supply the oil for the lamp, and by your fault that will come to pass which the Lord said: "for a blind man offering guidance to a blind man, both will fall into the pit." But also that will be fulfilled in you which the Lord said: "for if the light which is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness itself!" Therefore, that the light of knowledge may shine in the priests and their lamp may be always lit, do you fulfill your office, complete the commandment of God with regard to the services due to the priests. But if perhaps, having received from you the things which are necessary and "so not as of covetousness, but as of a blessing," they neglect to give their effort to instruction and to be free for the word of God and to "meditate on the law of God day and night," they themselves will see how they render an account to the Lord for your souls. But rather let us pray for the mercy of God almighty, that by his own light, his own truth, his own splendor he may deign to illuminate us all and to give "his word as a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths," our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is "the true light of the world," "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
Against Jovinianus 2.34

The whole account of the land of Judah and of the tribes is typical of the church in heaven. Let us read Joshua, the son of Nun, or the concluding portions of Ezekiel, and we shall see that the historical division of the land as related by the one finds a counterpart in the spiritual and heavenly promises of the other. What is the meaning of the seven and eight steps in the description of the temple? Or again, what significance attaches to the fact that in the Psalter, after being taught the mystic alphabet by the one hundred and eighteenth psalm we arrive by fifteen steps at the point where we can sing: "Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord: you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God." Why did two tribes and a half dwell on the other side of Jordan, a district abounding in cattle, while the remaining nine tribes and a half either drove out the old inhabitants from their possessions or dwelled with them? Why did the tribe of Levi receive no portion in the land but have the Lord for its portion? And how is it that of the priests and Levites, themselves, the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies where were the cherubim and the mercy seat? Why did the other priests wear linen raiment only, and not have their clothing of wrought gold, blue, scarlet, purple and fine cloth? The priests and Levites of the lower order took care of the oxen and carts; those of the higher order carried the ark of the Lord on their shoulders. If you do away with the gradations of the tabernacle, the temple, the church, if, to use a common military phrase, all upon the right hand are to be "up to the same standard," bishops are to no purpose, priests in vain, deacons useless. Why do virgins persevere? Widows toil? Why do married women practice continence? Let us all sin, and when once we have repented, we shall be on the same footing as the apostles.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 18.2

And let us see who it is that first received an inheritance from Jesus. "Caleb," it says, "the son of Jephunneh." For he is the first to ask, and he asks with certain definite reasons and words, which are written down; and these words can also instruct us unto salvation. First of all, Caleb is interpreted as "heart." Who then is, as it were, a heart, if not the one who in all things devotes his effort to the understanding, who is said to be no other member of the body of the church than that which is more excellent in us, the heart — that is, one who conducts all things with reason and prudence, and so administers everything as though he were nothing other than a heart? Now Jephunneh, his father, is interpreted "conversion." This Caleb, then, is the son of conversion; and why, unless because, having been turned to God, he brings forth from himself such fruit that the heart begets a son? Everyone, therefore, who has leisure for divine perceptions and does all things prudently and rationally is a Caleb. He, first indeed instructed by Moses, but secondly by Jesus, whom he attended, says: "you know the word which the Lord spoke to Moses the man of God." "You know the word which the Lord spoke." For who else can "know the word which the Lord spoke to Moses" except Jesus alone? No one understood the law as Jesus taught it; for he himself taught and opened up all things, he himself revealed to Paul that "the law is spiritual." "As he spoke," it says, "concerning me and concerning you." "Concerning me," it says, "and concerning you Moses spoke." "Concerning you" — this is what the Lord said: "if you believed Moses, you would surely also believe me; for he wrote of me." But when he said "concerning me" — that is, concerning Caleb, who is the heart — it is certain that Moses wrote concerning the heart, seeing that he wrote everything prudently and wisely. He says therefore: "today I am as strong as I was strong then." For the holy man is likewise "strong" both in things present and in things past, both in the new and in the old, both in the gospels and in the law. This, then, is what he says, that "he is strong today" under Jesus "as he was then" under Moses, because in the mysteries of both testaments the watchful heart is strong.
On the Duties of the Clergy 3.8.55-56

However, he [the Lord] said they should not come to that land which they had refused, as a penalty for their unbelief; but their children and wives, who had not murmured, and who, owing to their sex and age, were guiltless, should receive the promised inheritance of that land. So the bodies of those of twenty years old and upwards fell in the desert. The punishment of the rest was put aside. But they who had gone up with Joshua, and had thought fit to dissuade the people, died without delay of a great plague. Joshua and Caleb entered the land of promise together with those who were innocent by reason of age or sex. The better part, therefore, preferred glory to safety; the worse part safety to virtue. But the divine judgment approved those who thought virtue was above what is useful, while it condemned those who preferred what seemed more in accordance with safety than with what is virtuous.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 18.3

But let us also see his petition, which "Caleb, the son of Jephunneh," asked first from Jesus. "I ask of you," he says, "this mountain, as the Lord said in that day." The holy man seeks nothing lowly or base, nothing that lies in sunken valleys, but he seeks a lofty "mountain," and a "mountain" in which there are "great and fortified cities." For it is written: "there are the Anakim, cities great and fortified." And he was asking for these things because he knew how to wage war, as it is written: "the wise man occupied fortified cities and destroyed the stronghold in which the impious trusted." Do you suppose that, when Solomon said these things, he wished to teach us this — that "the wise man captured cities and destroyed strongholds" built of stones? Or does it rather indicate that the city and the walls are the dogmas of the impious and the syllogisms of the philosophers, by which they construct all manner of impious things contrary to the divine law, which are observed among the pagans or the barbarians? But those things too must be reckoned among these, and to be "fortified cities" and set upon mountains, which the heretics place in their assertions from the Scriptures as though upon high mountains. These "cities," then, every "wise man" who preaches the word of truth "has destroyed," and he has overthrown the cities of falsehood with the battering-ram of truth, just as the Apostle Paul also said: "destroying reasonings and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God." So then even now this most wise Caleb stands before Jesus and promises that "he is strong for war and ready for battle," and therefore he begs that there be permitted to him, as it were, the faculty of disputation, so that he may contend with the dialecticians of the world, with those who confirm falsehoods in place of truths, that he may refute and overcome them and overthrow all the things which they have constructed with their false assertions. And so at last, seeing his eagerness, "Jesus," it says, "blesses him" — namely, because he asks for and dares such things. But you too, if you are willing to give effort to your studies and to meditate prudently upon the law of God and to become a heart in the law of God, are able to overthrow those great and fortified cities, that is, the assertions of falsehood, so that you too may deserve to be blessed by Jesus and to receive Hebron from him.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 18.3

Now Hebron is interpreted "conjunction" or "wedlock." By this can perhaps be shown that thing — that the double cave purchased by the patriarch Abraham is there, in which the marriages of the fathers and their remains lie, that is, Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebecca, Jacob with Leah. Caleb, therefore, deserved to receive the remains of the fathers in his inheritance, without doubt because through the wisdom which was in him, by which he flourished both under Moses and under Jesus, he had understood the meaning of that very conjunction and had perceived what the cause was that with Abraham only Sarah lay there, and that neither Hagar nor Keturah deserved to be joined to him; or what the cause was that with Jacob only Leah seemed to lie, and neither Rachel, who had been more greatly beloved, nor any of the concubines had been united to him in the tomb. He himself, therefore, the prudent and wise Caleb, takes his inheritance among the memorials of the fathers. To him "Jesus assigned Hebron, the mother-city of the nation of the Anakim, and it becomes his lot unto this present day." Would that to me too there might be given the lot of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, and that my God might become mine, as he became "the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob," in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 19.1

Moses distributed the inheritance, and Jesus too distributed the inheritance. But it is not written in the distribution of Moses's inheritance that "the land rested from wars," whereas in the distribution of Jesus the very preface of the word begins thus: "and the land," it says, "rested from wars." If, then, you too wish to be made worthy to obtain an inheritance from Jesus, and to receive a portion from him, you must first bring all your wars to an end and stand fast in peace, so that of the land of your flesh also it may be said that "the land rested from wars."

n: Sin, or Sina, (ver. 3,) bordering upon Idumea, where the city of Cades-barne was situated, Numbers xiii. 22. It is now impossible to ascertain the precise situation of all the place mentioned in Scripture, as the land of Chanaan has been subject to so many changes. But this inconvenience attends all ancient geography. If those who attempt to unravel such labyrinths in profane authors, deserve praise, much more do those who do their utmost to explain the difficulties of sacred history. It was once very necessary to have the limits of the tribes marked out with precision, that, at the return from captivity, they might occupy their own. Now we may be satisfied if we can point out some of the places of the greatest importance. The limits of the tribe of Juda are specified with particular care, on account of the dignity and power of that tribe, which was to give kings to all the land, and a Messias to the world, as well as to preserve the true religion. The greatest part of the southern regions of Chanaan fell to their share, from the Dead Sea, by Idumea, to the Nile, and as far north as Jerusalem and the torrent of Cedron. (Calmet)
Bay, (lingua,) tongue. Chaldean, "a promontory," or rather a gulph. (Calmet)
Scorpion. A mountain infested with those creatures, by which people travelled from Idumea into Chanaan, leaving Sina on the left.
Asemona, which lies nearest to the river of Egypt of all the cities of Juda, Numbers xxxiv. 4., chap. xiii. 3.

Jordan, where it discharges itself into the Dead Sea, or mixes its waters with the latter; which, as we observe, (chap. v. 16,) does not take place for three miles. (Haydock) --- the north-western part of this sea belonged to Benjamin.
Stone. It is not certain that this was a city.

Galgal. Hebrew Gilgal, may designate "the limits." The valley of Achor lay south of Galgal. --- Sun. Hebrew, "Hen-Shemesh." It was not "a city." --- Rogel, "of the fuller." This fountain was in the king's gardens, running eastward from Sion into the torrent of Cedron. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] vii. 11.) It was used to wash linen. Rogel, signifies "to trample on," as they formerly washed their linen with their feet. Nausicrae is represented in Homer doing so, in holes or basins, prepared for the purpose. (Odyssey S)

Ennom. Hebrew, Ge-ben-Hinnom, or simply Ge-ennom, whence Gehenan has probably been formed. In this vale, children were immolated to Moloc: the beating of drums, to hinder their lamentations from being heard, caused it perhaps to be called Tophet. It was to the east of Jerusalem, (Calmet) inclining to the south. (Haydock) --- Northward. The valley extends south to Bethlehem. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] vii. 10.) Here David gained a great victory, 2 Kings v. 23. (Calmet) --- Woods. This explanation is added by St. Jerome. (Haydock) --- The ark remained at this city for some time, 1 Kings xv. 6. It was 10 miles north of Jerusalem.
Bethsames, "the house of the sun," was at the same distance, westward. Here the sight of the ark proved so fatal to 50,070 of the inhabitants, 1 Kings vi. 19. (Calmet)
Arbe, who was the father, and the greatest man of the race of Enac, chap. xiv. 15. (Haydock)
Enac. These three giants were at Hebron when the spies came thither, Numbers xiii.

Letters, as the Septuagint render it. St. Jerome adds this interpretation. (Haydock) --- It means literally "the city of the book." Senna, may also mean "instruction," ver. 49. Here probably a famous school was kept, before the arrival of the Israelites; or the archives of the nation might be deposited among these giants, as the Chaldean Kiriat-arche, "the city of the library, or archives," insinuates. (Bochart, Phaleg. ii. 17.)
Wife. Parents had full authority to do this. Saul promised his daughter to the person who should overcome Goliah. Something was required by way of dowry for the lady. (Grotius) (1 Kings xvii. 25.)

Brother. It is not clear in the original whether this relates to Cenez or to Othoniel, (Haydock) as younger is not found in [the] Hebrew but it is in the Syriac, Septuagint, and Judges i. 13. Many think that Cenez was the brother of Caleb. If Othoniel had been brother of the latter, they say he could not have legally married his niece. (Calmet) --- But though Moses forbids a nephew to marry his aunt, it does not follow that uncles could not take their nieces to wife, as they would be still the head; (Worthington) whereas there would be a sort of indecency for a nephew to command his aunt. The Jews allow these marriages, while the Samaritans condemn them, Leviticus xviii. 14. In confirmation of the Vulgate, we may remark, that Cenez is never (Calmet) clearly (Haydock) represented as the brother of Caleb; and there is no inconvenience in asserting that Othoniel was the brother of the latter, whether we take this word to denote a near relation, or strictly. In the former supposition, Othoniel might marry his cousin, Axa, the daughter of Caleb, while he himself was descended from Cenez, the brother of Jephone. (Calmet) --- But if we take the word strictly, as the remark of his being younger brother, both here and Judges i. 13., may seem to imply, we must then allow that Othoniel followed the custom of his nation, (Haydock) in marrying his niece. (Menochius) --- Septuagint here make him "the younger son of Cenez, who was brother of Caleb;" and in the Book of Judges, they say, "Gothoniel, the son of Cenez, (and) the younger brother of Caleb, first made himself master of it, under him;" as if Othoniel and Caleb had been born of the same mother, but of a different father, unless we suppose that they were only nearly related, and the former much less advanced in years; so that he might well marry the daughter of Caleb and afterwards become a judge and deliverer of Israel, Judges iii. 9. See Masius; Bonfrere. (Haydock)

Was moved; as the Syriac, Arabic, Junius, &c., represent the matter. Others render the Hebrew in a different sense: "she moved him to ask of her father a field, and she lighted off her ass, and Caleb said unto her," &c., which seems very abrupt, as she herself is represented as soliciting for the favour in the next verse, instead of her husband. The Chaldean supposes that she was restrained by natural modesty, from preferring the petition; but when Othoniel refused to do it, or was denied what he requested, she took courage and asked herself. The sense of the Vulgate seems more natural, (Calmet) as the husband might easily suppose that she would have greater influence with her father. (Haydock) --- Sighed. The original term is found only in this history, and in that of the death of Sisara, Judges iv. 21. Septuagint, "she cried out." Others translate, "she remained fixed," (Menochius) or "she waited sitting on the ass," till she had obtained her request.

Blessing, or "favour, present," &c., 1 Kings xxv. 27. (Calmet) --- And dry. This is a farther explanation of southern; as the lands in that situation being exposed to the sun-beams, in Palestine, are often destitute of sufficient moisture, which is the cause of the sterility of Mount Hebal, &c. --- Watery ground. Hebrews, "springs of water, and he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs." Aquila leaves springs untranslated. (Haydock) --- Golgot. Septuagint, "Golathmaim, and the upper Golath," &c. Symmachus translates "possession on the high places," Judges i. (Calmet) --- Caleb had probably given his daughter a part of the mountain. He now grants her also some field that lay lower down, and was better supplied with water on all sides (Haydock) by springs above, and cisterns below.

New Asor, to distinguish it from the capital of Jabin, in the north. This was dependent on Ascalon. (Eusebius) --- Hebrew, "and Hazor, Hadatta, and (or) Kerioth ("the towns") of Hezron, which is Hazor." The Septuagint only specify the same town of Asor by different names. There was one towards Arabia, Numbers xi. 35.

Bersabee, noted for the residence of Abraham, &c. It is attributed to Simeon, (chap. xix. 2,) with some other of these towns, as the two tribes lived intermixed, and some changes might be made in the first regulation, to bring things to a greater equality, and as circumstances might require.
Siceleg. The Philistines kept possession of it till king Achis gave it to David; and it continued afterwards the property of the kings of Juda.

Villages. Twenty-nine of the former cities were of greater note; the six, or taking in the three belonging to Caleb, the nine others which are mentioned, (Calmet) were only villages. (Menochius) --- Others think that these nine towns are not numbered here, because they were allotted to the tribe of Simeon, chap. xix. 2, &c.
Plains. Hebrew Schephela, near Eleutheropolis, chap. x. 40. --- Estaol was afterwards given to Dan. Samson was buried near it and Sarea, Judges xvi.
Fourteen. One of those mentioned above, may have been a village. (Menochius) --- Others think that Enaim may be the name of a fountain, near which perhaps Juda met Thamar, Genesis xxxviii. 14.
Ceila, which David took from the Philistines, and were he was nearly betrayed into the hands of Saul, 1 Kings xxiii. Habacuc was buried here, on the road between Eleutheropolis and Hebron.
Carmel. Not where Elias dwelt, but a city and mountain 10 miles east of Eleutheropolis. Nabal rendered it famous by his imprudence, (1 Kings xxv.) and Saul by a triumphal arch, 1 Kings xv. 12.

Bessur. About 20 miles from Jerusalem, fortified by Simon, 1 Machabees xiv. 33. It is there said to be only five stadia distant from that city. But the Alexandrian copy reads five schœnus, or cords, each of which consisted of at least 30 stadia. (Cellarius)

Eltecon: given afterwards to the tribe of Dan, (chap. xix. 44,) and then to the Levites, chap. xxi. 13. The Alexandrian Septuagint here add many cities, which are omitted in Hebrew. (Calmet) --- "Theco and Ephrata, (this is Bethlehem) and Phagor, and Artam, and Koulon, and Tatami, and Sores, and Karem, and Gallim, and Baither, and Manocho, eleven cities and their villages." (Haydock) See St. Jerome in Micheas v. 1. (Calmet) (Deuteronomy xxvii. 4.) --- Dr. Wall says, "these cities were doubtless in the Hebrew copy of the Septuagint" and "they are of such a nature, that it is scarcely possible to think them an interpolation." The former critic thinks "the omission in the Hebrew was occasioned by the word villages occurring immediately before, and at the end of the words thus omitted; and indeed the same word occurring in different places, has been the cause of many and great omissions in the Hebrew manuscripts. He thinks it less likely that the Jews should have designedly omitted Bethlehem here, because that place is mentioned as belonging to Juda, in several other parts of Scripture." But is Ephrata ever joined with it, except in this passage, and in the text of Micheas? "And, therefore, though this remarkable omission was probably owing, at first, to some transcriber's mistake, its not being reinserted might be owing to the reason specified by St. Jerome, out of malice to Christianity." (Kennicott, 2 Diss. 56.) --- Reland is astonished to find a place which was to be rendered so famous by the birth of the Messias, not enumerated in this place among the cities of Juda. But he observes that it is found in the Alexandrian version, p. 643. (Palest.) --- St. Jerome will not decide absolutely whether the Jews have erased these cities, or the Septuagint have inserted them. As he undertook to translate the Hebrew as he found it, he has not admitted these cities into his translation, though there seems to be abundant reason for supposing that they are genuine. (Haydock)

Salt. Bonfrere supposes it is Segor, which was preserved for Lot's sake. --- Engaddi, which was famous for its balm and palm-trees, in the desert of Jericho. (Solin. xxxv.) --- We may here remark that in the preceding catalogues, many towns are repeated like Zanoe, (ver. 34., and 56,) and others are left out. Some are also afterwards attributed to other tribes. Hence some have inferred that alterations have been made in the original copies. But we may rather believe that the reason of these variations is, because the cities were parcelled out among the 10 families of Juda, (1 Paralipomenon ii. 3,) as was the case in the distribution of land to Manasses; (chap. xvii. 2,) and hence the same cities were sometimes given to two different families. They are also attributed to different tribes, because many families of the respective tribes dwelt in them. The priests, for example, lived along with their brethren of other tribes. (Calmet)

Jerusalem. The Benjamites claimed the northern part of this city; (Haydock) and they did not drive out the Jebusites, but lived with them, Judges i. 21. The tribe of Juda had burnt a part of the city, Judges i. 8. But it seems the Jebusites kept their hold, (Calmet) at least in the citadel, (Haydock) and frequently in the lower town, till they were entirely banished by David, 2 Kings v. 7. See Judges xix. 11. In latter times, the Jews considered this place as the common city of all the nation, to which none of the tribes had an exclusive right; and hence, in the last siege, there was no head, and all the Jews were admitted without examination. (Josephus, Jewish Wars iv. 5, &c.) (Calmet) --- Day, and even till the reign of David. The author of this observation must have lived before that period. Josue might have made this and many other similar remarks, when he finished this work, towards the end of his life. (Haydock)

f: HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 19.2

Then, further, since it is the custom of holy Scripture to name the four regions of the world, which they call either poles or zones, in the description of "the borders of the tribe of Judah" only two are named and two are passed over in silence. For it is written thus: "and the borders of the tribe of the sons of Judah according to their peoples were from the borders of Idumaea, from the desert of Sin toward the west." And when it had described the borders on the west, it then says: "and on the east all the salt sea," and it passed over the other two regions in silence, that is, the north and the south. See, therefore, whether these things are not filled with mysteries. Although we cannot perceive or explain each one, nevertheless, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it and we are able to grasp it, we will attempt to examine each single point. "The borders of Judah," it says, "were according to their peoples from the borders of Idumaea, from the desert of Sin toward the west." Therefore "the borders of Judaea" are next to "the borders of Idumaea." Now "Idumaea," as we have often already said, is interpreted "earthly." After the earthly things, then, "the borders of Judaea" immediately follow. But it also says "from the desert of Sin." And "Sin" is interpreted "temptations." After the temptations, then, follow "the borders" of the inheritance "of Judaea." The "west" and the "east" are named, and those neighboring places which we mentioned above, indeed the bordering regions. But also "the valley of Egypt" is designated as neighboring to the western parts, which is "from the desert toward the west," while "on the east" the "borders" are girded "by the salt sea."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 19.3

After this it says "from the hills that stretch toward the west; and thence one ascends from the west as far as Cades Barne," and thus it stretches from the west "to the west of Cades." And these are their borders on the southwest, and thence it went on "as far as the valley of Egypt." Do you see how in the western parts it names both the "southwest" and "Egypt" and the sunset? Without doubt, so that each one may know that all these things must be escaped and passed through by him, so that at last he may thus be able to arrive at the royal tribe, of which the Apostle says: "it is evident, moreover, that our Lord arose from Judah." Now "from the borders of Idumaea" is "the desert of Sin." A little earlier we said of the desert of Sin that it signifies temptations, and therefore it is necessary for us to pass through the wilderness of temptations, so that we may thus be able to arrive at the inheritance of the sons of Judah. But it is also necessary for us "to ascend the ascent of the hills of Acrabin," which is interpreted "scorpions." We must therefore also pass through and "tread upon" even the "scorpions," those, without doubt, of which the Savior says: "behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions." Whoever, then, wishes and desires to enter into the inheritance of the tribe of Judah must ascend these ascents and "tread upon" and escape the "scorpions" that stand in the way. Whence I think that it was to a man making this journey that the Lord also said to the prophet Ezekiel: "son of man, you dwell in the midst of scorpions." "And the borders are," it says, "as far as Cades." "Cades" is interpreted "holy" or "sanctification." The "borders" of Judah, therefore, reach as far as sanctification.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 19.4

But let us also see what "the borders on the eastern side" are. Not that I now wish to make a catalogue of places, but that we may contemplate the images of the mysteries which are signified through these things. It is said, then, that "on the eastern side of the tribe of Judah" is "the salt sea," and after this in its region is named "the fountain of the sun" and "the city of the sun," and that in the same tribe there is also "the city of letters." It is necessary, therefore, that everyone who wishes to enter into the portion of the sons of Judah first cross "the salt sea," that is, overcome the waves and whirlwinds of this life, and escape all those things which in this world, because of their uncertainty and slipperiness, are compared to the waves of the sea, so that he may be able to arrive at the land of Judah and to approach "the fountain of the sun." But what is "the fountain of the sun," or of which "sun"? Of that one, without doubt, of whom it is written: "but to those who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall arise." Of this "sun," then, if you first escape "the salt sea," you will find "the fountain" in the land of Judah. Which "fountain"? That one, assuredly, of which Jesus said: "but whoever drinks of the water that I give him, there shall be made in him a fountain of water springing up into life eternal." When, therefore, you have found such a "fountain" of this "sun" as we have described, you will also find his "city." "For there is also there," it says, "a city of the sun." There is said to be in Egypt also a "city of the sun." But that "city" which is in Egypt received the name of this "sun," whom "the heavenly Father bids to rise upon the good and the evil." But that city which is in Judaea is made up of the saints only, because it is the "city of God," and that fountain, of which we spoke above, being made "a river, gladdens the city of God." But you too, if you are fortified on every side and surrounded by the wall of continence, if you are strengthened by the towers of wisdom and magnanimity, you too will be made a "city of God." But if to all these things you add for yourself the light of knowledge, as Isaiah said: "kindle for yourselves the light of knowledge," and the "sun of righteousness" shines upon you, you too will be made a "city of the sun," or you will receive "the city of the sun" as the lot of your inheritance. But also, if you hand yourself over to the law of God and "meditate" upon it "day and night," and "the book of the law shall not depart from your hand," as is said to Jesus, and if you are mindful of the precept of the Savior, in which he says "search the Scriptures" — if, then, you devote yourself to such pursuits and obtain the instruction of the divine law either by reading or by hearing, then "the city of letters" is made part of your portion. And these things indeed we have examined according to the possibility of our own understanding, or also according to the capacity of your hearing; but the fullness of knowledge and the deeper and clearer understanding of these things will belong to those who deserve to obtain the true "inheritance" of the true and only-begotten Son of God, which has been promised "to those who love him" perfectly, in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 20.3

But now, since there is not sufficient time for us to discuss all the things that have been read, we will touch briefly on at least a few, as the Lord shall grant. The beginning of distributing the inheritance which Jesus distributed begins from Caleb. For to this Caleb was given the lot of his portion before his tribe, which is that of the sons of Judah, received it, and it is given to him not in some outermost parts, but in the midst of the sons of Judah; and there was given to him a portion not by lot, but by the command of the Lord, and there is given to him an entire city. What other person was worthy to obtain such an inheritance and to receive such a portion, except Caleb, who alone was preserved safe together with Jesus of Nave out of the six hundred thousand armed men who had gone out from Egypt? It was fitting that he himself should receive the "metropolis." And therefore it is written: "Jesus gave him the city of Arboc, the metropolis of Enac, which is Hebron," in which were the memorials of the fathers. This man therefore, having received "the city of Arboc, which was the metropolis of Enac, which is Hebron, exterminated from there the three sons of Enac." What do you suppose Scripture, wishing to show us, also designated this — that Caleb, having received the portion of his inheritance, "exterminated the three sons of Enac," and described their names, that is, "Susi and Achima and Thalami, the generations of Enac"? Let us see, therefore, what it means that it does not suffice for it to say "the sons of Enac," but it has added also their very names, and above all appended: "these were the generations of Enac." But in what follows it also relates that Caleb, having received the lot of his inheritance, "went up to those who dwelt in Dabir; but the name of Dabir was formerly the city of letters." It must be seen, therefore, what it means that it "was formerly the city of letters" and afterward was made "Dabir."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 20.5

First, therefore, let us examine why Caleb received the "metropolis," and that one which, first among all the others in the land of promise, is named "metropolis." And "the metropolis of Enac" — "Enac" is interpreted as empty humility or empty answer. Caleb therefore received the "metropolis" of empty humility. It is certain that there are two humilities. One praiseworthy, of which the Savior says: "learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls." And of this humility it is said that "everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted," and elsewhere: "humble yourselves therefore under the most mighty hand of God." But there is also another, culpable humility of sinners, such as that which Scripture speaks of concerning unlawful intercourse, that "he humbled" her — as is written of Ammon, that he "humbled" Thamar his sister. There is therefore an empty humility which descends from sin. Of this empty humility, then, Caleb "took the metropolis" — or "cut it off" — "and slew the three sons of Enac," who were the sons of empty humility, and, they being killed, he himself inhabits the city and does the things which are written in what follows. But who are these sons of empty humility, whom "Caleb exterminated"? The first is "Susi," which is interpreted as outside me, that is, outside the holy one, because the son of empty humility is outside the holy one, indeed even outside God. There is another, "Achiman," which is interpreted as my brother outside counsel, as if we were to say, a brother without counsel. For it is certain that all the brothers who are born of empty humility are also outside counsel. The third is "Thalami," which is interpreted as a precipice or a hanging, which designates that there is nothing of stability in him, but that all things are wavering and rushing headlong. These "three sons of Enac," then, Caleb "exterminated and killed," and after them "he went up into Dabir." "The name of Dabir was formerly the city of letters." "Dabir" is interpreted as speech. But "the name of Dabir was formerly the city of letters." Therefore understand as "the city of letters" the whole instrument of the Old Testament — that is, let us understand even this very scripture, which we are now trying to expound, to be "the city of letters," which afterward is made "Dabir," which is speech. For these things, which formerly were in letters and were understood according to the letter, now in the churches of Christ, by the Lord's revelation, have been made speech, since the holy Apostles first speak of it and discourse upon it, and remove the surface of the letter, but bring forth from it a spiritual speech. But the individual teachers of the churches also make the letter of the law into an evangelical speech and discussion. But who are the "three sons of Enac," whom "Caleb" — in whose person we had ascribed the power of the law — "slays"? The empty humility must be taken as that which all the poets or philosophers of this world thought concerning the divinity, since the things they thought are both lowly and unworthy of God. For what is so lowly and what so emptily lowly as either to set up "wood and stones" as gods or to think them such? Of this empty humility, then, the first son is he who is called outside me, that is, their first notion is both outside the truth and outside God. But the second is "Achiman," that is, a brother without counsel: for it is certain that this too is a brother of that error which is carried on without counsel. For what is so without counsel as to forsake God, who made us, and to follow those whom we ourselves made? The third notion of error is "Thalami," which is a precipice or a hanging. For the last stages of this error tend toward the precipice and the depth of hell. These notions of gentile-worship, then, as "sons of Enac" of the ancient error, the law cuts off, which even according to the letter proclaims "the true God" and "the creator of all things."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 20.4

Moreover it is related that Caleb, having a daughter, proposed a certain condition of this kind, saying: "whoever shall be able to cut off the city of letters and to obtain it, to him I will give Ascha my daughter as wife." And when he had proposed this, "Gothoniel the son of Cenez, the younger brother of Caleb, took the city of letters." But this too holy Scripture has set as a question, if indeed, as we have said, nothing in these words is to be passed over idly — that "Gothoniel" is said to be the "brother of Caleb," and "Caleb" is written as "the son of Ieffone," and "Gothoniel the son of Cenez." How then will he seem to be the "brother of Caleb," who is not "the son of Ieffone," but the one is called "the son of Ieffone," while the other is "the son of Cenez," who is said "to have taken the city of letters"? Of whom it is added that he was also "the younger," and by the condition, deservedly for his virtue, "received Ascha the daughter of Caleb as wife," because he "cut off and destroyed the city of letters." But Ascha, "going out" from the house of her father, who was "given in marriage" to him by a fixed condition, sitting upon an "ass," said to her husband: "I will ask of my father a portion of a field; and she cried out from the mountain. And Caleb said to her: what is it with you? And she said to him: give me a blessing, since you have given me in marriage into the land of the south. And she received the upper Gonetla and the lower Gonetla." And Scripture concludes on these things, saying: "this is the inheritance of the tribe of Judah." You see that there is truly need of the help of God, that these things may be explained; and it is utterly impossible for any of men to discourse of these things, unless he has been illuminated through the grace of God. Therefore, then, help me with your prayers and labor together with me, that the Lord may deign to show us the light of truth in these places so obscure and hidden, so that we too may be able to open to you how these things are true and useful and divine, but, on account of the frailty of human nature, are covered over with sacraments and enveloped in mysteries.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 20.6

But now "Caleb went up to" that "city of letters and said": "whoever shall cut off the city of letters and obtain it, to him I will give Ascha my daughter as wife. And Gothoniel the son of Cenez took it." Now "Gothoniel," who received the "city of letters," is interpreted as the answer of God. But he can be called the answer of God to whom God answers, that is, to whom he reveals secrets and discloses hidden things. This, then, is he who can "receive the city of letters" of the old instrument and "cut off" "the letter that kills," "the younger brother of Caleb." But I, from the Church, am "the younger brother of Caleb," who, when the letter of the law has been cut off and shaken out, seek in it the spiritual sense. And I "cut off" "the letter" when I am no longer circumcised according to the flesh, nor eat the unleavened bread according to the flesh, nor observe the passover with the Jews, nor keep the sabbath according to the letter. For it was promised to me that, if I "cut off the city of letters," I would receive the daughter of my elder brother. For I was formerly "the son of Cenez," which is interpreted as contempt. For who was contempt, as we "gentiles, alienated from the manner of life of Israel, having no hope and without God in this world"? For that former brother of mine, whose daughter I now receive for this, that I "cut off the city of letters," he was "the son of Ieffone," which is interpreted as conversion. He therefore "gives" me his "daughter," that is, the law gives to me, the younger brother, the knowledge of itself or the understanding of itself, according to what is written: "the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and shall be given to a nation producing its fruits." Yet it must be known that the law, to which we have now given the person of Caleb, is one thing, and the letter of the old testament, which we have figuratively called "the city of letters," is another. Having received his daughter, then, I, "his younger brother," lead her out from the house of her father. And when she comes with me, sitting upon an "ass" — upon what "ass"? that one, without doubt, which "the disciples had loosed" of the Savior — she "says" to her father: "give me a blessing, father. And she received the upper Gonetla and the lower Gonetla." Which the Apostle says more plainly: "having the promise of life, both of that which now is and of that which is to come"; and as the Savior promises to those who follow the perfection of his word, that "they receive a hundredfold" in the present age, but in the future obtain "eternal life." This, then, is "to have received in blessing the upper Gonetla and the lower Gonetla." Which "blessing" let us pray that we too may deserve to attain, through Christ our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 21.1

"The sons of Judah" wished "to drive out" or "to destroy" "the Jebusites from Jerusalem, and they could not"; on account of which "the Jebusites dwelt with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem down to the present day." Beginning from the letter, we wish to inquire of those who suppose that these things can stand according to the letter, what is meant when it says "down to the present day" — a phrase that holy Scripture always employs to signify by it the eternity of the age, as when it says: "do not depart from the Lord on this present day," that is, as long as the age stands. Let them show me, then, how the "Jebusite," as long as the age stands, "dwells with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem," seeing that not even the "sons of Judah" themselves "dwell in Jerusalem." Therefore neither can this be true, that "the Jebusites dwell with the Jews in Jerusalem," since not even they themselves dwell in it. But let us understand these things spiritually, taking up the parable of the Gospel which says concerning the "tares": "let both grow together, lest perchance, when you wish to root up the tares, you root up together with them the wheat also." As therefore in the Gospel "the tares are permitted to grow together with the wheat," in the same way here too in Jerusalem, that is, in the church, there are certain "Jebusites," those who lead an ignoble and degenerate life, who are perverse both in faith and in deeds and in their whole manner of conduct. For it is not possible that the church be purged to clarity while it is on earth, so that neither any impious person nor any sinner may be seen to remain in it, but that all in it be holy and blessed and in whom no stain of sin at all may be caught. But just as it is said concerning the "tares": "lest perchance, in rooting up the tares, you root up together with them the wheat also," so also it can be said concerning those in whom there are either doubtful or hidden sins. For we do not say concerning those who are manifestly and evidently criminal, that they should not be expelled from the church. Hear then the Scripture saying that: "the sons of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, but they dwelt with them in Jerusalem down to the present day." Wherefore I beseech you who are faithful, that you so keep your life and conduct that you neither yourselves suffer scandal in anything nor cause scandal to others; but let it be to you a matter of highest zeal and highest caution, lest anyone polluted enter into this holy congregation of yours, lest any Jebusite dwell with you. For you see that the Scripture says that "the sons of Judah could not cast out the Jebusites from Jerusalem." Now "Jebusite" is interpreted as trampling. Grant, then, that we cannot "cast out" those who trample us: let us at least cast out those whom we can, whose sins are manifest. For where sin is not evident, we can "cast out" no one from the church, "lest perchance in rooting up the tares we root up together with them the wheat also."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 21.2

Yet it moves me that it said that they "could not cast out the Jebusites," that is, those who are interpreted as trampling. And therefore let us see who they are in the church that trample. Those, without doubt, of whom the Lord spoke in the Gospels: "do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor your pearls before swine, lest perchance they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you to pieces." This, then, is the "Jebusite," the trampling, those who unworthily hear the word of God and, when they have heard it, neither depart as unbelievers nor remain as believers, but, having received the knowledge of the mysteries and having scrutinized the more secret things of our faith, "turning" afterward attack us, and by their contradictions "tear apart" our hearts, "trampling" the "pearls" of the Lord's word and staining the ornaments of faith. Concerning these, then, it is said that "the sons of Judah could not cast out the Jebusite from Jerusalem down to the present day." Something similar is written also concerning Ephraim; for the Scripture says: "and Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanite, who dwelt in Gazer; and the Canaanite dwelt in Ephraim down to the present day." "Ephraim" is interpreted as fructification. He therefore who bears fruit and grows in faith "cannot exterminate the Canaanite," the worst seed, the accursed seed, the seed ever shifting, ever uncertain; for this is what "Canaanite" is interpreted to mean. And it is certain that with him who bears fruit and grows, the "Canaanite" always "dwells"; for the stirrings of temptations never cease from him. But if you truly bear fruit in God and see someone of this sort restless, turbulent, shifting, know that he is a "Canaanite." And if you cannot cast him out of the church, because "the sons of Ephraim could not drive out the Canaanites," observe that which the Apostle admonishes, saying: "withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks restlessly." But since Solomon urges that "these things which we read be written on the heart in threefold manner," that also, besides those things which we have said, which occurs to my heart, I shall bring forth to your ears, and do you that which is written, that while one speaks the rest may examine. While I therefore speak what I feel, do you discern and examine whether it is right or less than right. Concerning Jerusalem we have frequently said that it is interpreted as vision of peace. If therefore in our heart Jerusalem has been built, that is, if the vision of peace has been founded in our heart and we always gaze upon Christ, who is "our peace," and keep him in our heart — if indeed we are so fixed and stable in this vision of peace that never at all does any evil thought or counsel of any sin ascend into our heart, if this could so come to pass, we could say that we are in Jerusalem and that no other dwells with us except only those who are holy. But now, since — even if we come to great progress and cultivate ourselves with the highest zeal — nevertheless I do not think that so much purity comes to anyone's heart that he is never stained by the contagion of an adverse thought, it is certain that "the Jebusites also dwell with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem." Yet we do not say these things in order that we should neglect, as much as can be done, to "cast them out," but we must labor enough and attempt daily to "cast them out" of Jerusalem; but, as it is written, we cannot "cast out" all of them at once. And this same thing must also be understood concerning those who bear fruit, who are named sons of "Ephraim," who likewise ought always to cast out of their souls the "Canaanites," the wandering and slippery thoughts. But God is able, who may subject to us both the "Jebusites" and the "Canaanites," as it is written: "and he subjected the Canaanites to the sons of Ephraim." Let us therefore beseech the Lord himself, that, casting from us "evil thoughts," he may bring in good ones, worthy of "Jerusalem the heavenly city," in which nothing polluted or filthy may be found, which might accuse us on the day of judgment from the thoughts of conscience, but that there may be found in us purity of heart in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

n: Joseph. The double portion is given to him, as Ruben forfeited his birth-right. (Chaldean) (Worthington) --- Waters; or the celebrated fountain, which renders the territory so fruitful, and which was made sweet, by Eliseus casting salt into it, 4 Kings ii. 19. --- Wilderness of Bethaven, chap. xviii. 12., and viii. 14. (Calmet) --- Which, is not to be referred to wilderness, but to the word lot. (Masius; Menochius)

To Luza. The Vulgate reads Bethel Luza, which may be supposed to be two names, (chap. xviii. 13.; Haydock) for the same city. (Menochius) (Genesis xxviii. 29.) --- Bethel was probably the country, (Calmet) or mountain, (Haydock) to the east of Luza, on the frontiers of Benjamin and of Ephraim; for which reason it is sometimes attributed to both. --- To Atharoth. This city, and Archi, are supposed by some to be the same city. Archi seems, however, to have been a distinct place, where Chusai ws born, 2 Kings xv. 32. Atharoth is styled Addar, "the illustrious," ver. 5. It was 15 miles from Jericho.
Nether. See chap. x. 11. The upper Bethoron was of much less note, near the Jordan. --- Gazer was in the vicinity of Azotus, 1 Machabees xiv. 34., chap. x. 33. (Calmet)
Possessed it, or divided the country between them. The territories of Ephraim are henceforward described, to the end of the chapter. (Menochius)

Looketh to the north, &c. The meaning is, that the border went towards the north, by Machmethath; and then turned eastward to Thanathselo. (Challoner) --- Borders. It should be terminus. "The border turneth eastward," Septuagint. (Bonfrere) --- Janoe, twelve miles east of Sichem. (Eusebius) (4 Kings xv. 29.)

Reeds. Septuagint, "of Cana." The vale belonged to Manasses, but the cities were ceded to Ephraim, ver. 9., chap. xvii. 19. The limits of these two tribes are very confused. (Calmet) --- Most salt. This is the title generally applied to the lake of Sodom. But here the Mediterranean is meant, which, compared with many of the seas of Palestine, is certainly most salt. (Menochius) --- The epithet is not, however, found in Hebrew or Septuagint (Calmet) and Serarius thinks it has crept in here by mistake. (Menochius)

Gazer. It is not certain when the Ephraimites rendered this city tributary, or when it threw off the yoke. The king of Egypt afterwards conquered it, and gave it with his daughter to Solomon, chap. x. 33. (Calmet) See Judges i. 29. --- The negligence of Ephraim was contrary to God's order, Exodus xx. (Menochius) --- The Alexandrian Septuagint here inserts after day, "till Pharao, king of Egypt, went up and took the city, and burnt it with fire, and the Chanaanites and Pherezites, and the inhabitants of Gazer, he slew; and Pharao gave it as a dowry to his daughter." Grabe adds what seems deficient, "and they became tributary slaves." (Haydock)

HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 22.1

The "Canaanites" are said, for the third time, to be among the sons of Ephraim. But let us observe what is the order of these statements in each case, that is, what the first statement contains, which says that the Canaanites were with the sons of Ephraim, and what the second and the third contain. For if we observe more carefully how the Canaanites are said to be with the sons of Ephraim for the third time, then, by the Lord's help, we shall be able to investigate the order of the statements — what is reported to have been done from this in the first, what in the second, what in the third — and I think we shall not be unbelieving that these things were truly written not merely that the narrative of the deeds should be handed down to us by itself, but that they were filled with divine mysteries worthy of God. First, then, it was said that: "Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanite who dwelt in Gazer; but the Canaanite dwelt in Ephraim until this present day, and he was made a servant under tribute, until Pharaoh king of Egypt came up and took the city and burned it with fire, and slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites and those who dwelt in Gazer; and Pharaoh gave it as a dowry to his daughter." Second: "and it came to pass," it says, "when the sons of Israel had grown strong, that they made the Canaanites subject, but by extermination they did not exterminate them." Third, when the men of the tribe of Ephraim "contradicted Jesus," wishing, according to their multitude — because they were many and strong — to receive also a greater portion of the inheritance, and they are commanded to "go up into the forest" and make more room for themselves; and, that they might be able to occupy wider spaces, they are commanded to "exterminate the Canaanite."
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 22.2

Let us see, then, now, what this threefold narrative concerning the Canaanites means. First, the "Canaanite" is indeed with us and is "under tribute," yet he is not obedient to us nor a "servant." Second, he is made even a "servant" and obedient. Let us here take the Canaanite as our flesh, or the things that belong to the flesh. This is first with us, that is, it is joined to the soul, but it is not obedient to it, except only that it "pays tribute," that is, it does indeed furnish the service of doing or moving something, "yet it lusts against the spirit" and is not obedient to the soul, but yields to its own desires. But if we have now made some progress, the flesh "is made" for us a "servant" and obedient, and submitting to the will of the soul; and this is the second progress of the soul, when it has made the flesh both obey it and serve it. The third, however, is that which is perfect. For if we now come to the perfect, the "Canaanite" is said to be "exterminated" by us and handed over to death. But how this is fulfilled in our flesh, hear the Apostle saying: "mortify your members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness," and the rest that follows. And again he says: "but they who are Christ's have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts." So then, thirdly, that is, when we come to perfection and "mortify our members" and "carry about the death of Christ in our body," the "Canaanite" is said to be "exterminated" by us.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 22.3

But this too is not to be passed over idly, that it is said that "Pharaoh came and took the city of Gazer, in which the Canaanite dwelt with Ephraim, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter." Now "Gazer" is interpreted as constriction. If, therefore, body and soul dwell in one and the same constriction, that is, joined and allied to one another, so that the soul both lives carnally and does not hasten to make the flesh more swiftly obedient and subject to itself, it is to be feared lest "Pharaoh come" out of Egypt and lead the unhappy soul captive, so that he "hands her over as a dowry to his daughter." For if you consider that which the Apostle said, that "another law arises in our members and leads us captive under the law of sin," you will find how that Pharaoh, who is the author and king of sin, "enrolls as a dowry" for "his daughter," who is "the law of sin," the soul that has lived carnally.
